We're now just over a week away from the launch of GTA 6, the first new game from Rockstar since Red Dead Redemption 2, and the first new entry in the Grand Theft Auto series since GTA 5. It's been a long, long wait for the studio's latest big game, but it seems Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick is already willing to tease Rockstar's next project.

"Rockstar has completed the development of GTA 6," Zelnick tells investors during Take-Two's latest financial results call. "That may not come as a surprise to you, since we're 10 days away from the release. They have done their very best work, and it’s going to come to consumers soon. They're in the middle of their marketing campaign, which also, unsurprisingly, is fully baked. At this point, it’s the job of the organization to make sure that we do an A+ job, technically, in delivering this product to consumers."

Zelnick concludes: "Then, of course, Rockstar will focus on what comes next, and they'll announce that in the fullness of time."

So… what does come next for Rockstar? The obvious guess would be a new version of GTA Online. The existing online game generates unfathomable profits, so a follow-up would seem inevitable even if it hadn't leaked as part of Rockstar's ongoing union dispute. But Rockstar and Take-Two have resolutely refused to even hint at what the next generation of GTA Online will entail.

During the financial call Q&A, Zelnick deftly dodged multiple questions alluding to GTA Online. He's not worried about players running out of content in GTA 6, for example, because "there's so much to be done in all things Grand Theft Auto." He's also not particularly concerned about the recent wave of jailbreaks affecting the future of GTA Online,

GTA 6 launch files already hint at online multiplayer, PlayStation Store sleuth reports, leading to hopes we won't be waiting for a GTA Online follow-up for long

#3798. Former Rockstar Games tech director thinks GTA 6 could be coming to PC sooner than you'd expect to curb AI clones

Former Rockstar Games North technical director Obbe Vermeij believes that the possibility of AI vibe coded ports of Grand Theft Auto 6 could push Rockstar to create an official PC version sooner than you'd expect.

Speaking to RockPaperShotgun as part of a wider interview, Vermeij said generative AI "really has changed the world.". He elaborated: "I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC, which won't be as good as [the developer's] effort, but it could still also hurt their sales. So, I wouldn't be surprised if there was an effort to get [the releases] a little bit closer together."

Vermeij emphasised that he doesn't know what Rockstar's plans are, but with his technical expertise, he does believe that generative AI tools are "probably" capable of pulling off a GTA 6 PC port.

"It will take a long time. It actually, physically takes hours and hours and hours to do these things," Vermeij said. "And it will take a bunch of tokens and everything, so it would probably cost like, tens of thousands of dollars in tokens. But like, you know, if it's GTA, I think people are gonna try it.".

We've already seen people thrust footage of Grand Theft Auto 6 into AI software over the past few months. AI slop videos have been pulling in millions of views on social media, and people have been 'improving' trailer footage with Nvidia's DLSS5 'yassification' machine (thanks Ars Technica). Grand Theft Auto 6 itself will not feature any generative AI or microtransactions at launch.

AI game clones continue to be a problem. Game developers have cancelled public demos in fear of having their game copied, and Steam owner Valve has gone out to say it's the developer's responsibility to prevent cloning by making their games more original. Even as Anthropic has introduced measures to prevent such practices, other AI software can still perform such tasks.

#3797. Sick BMX flips, colourful characters, a whole lot of mail and a charming raccoon dog await you in Tanuki: Pon's Summer, which you can pick up now

Right, today's been miserable thanks to the now hourly discourse we have to all take part in lest we be seen as approving of the current bad thing, how about something that looks simply pleasant? Today's the launch day for Tanuki: Pon's Summer, a delightfully vibrant mail delivery sim/Tony Hawk's Pro Skater but for bikes about restoring a shrine before the end of summer.

I've been enamoured by the vibe of Tanuki: Pon's Summer since it was announced in no small part because of how in some small ways it reminds me of Boku No Natsuyasumi, a cult-classic, Japan-only game series that's mostly just about hanging out in the Japanese countryside. This one isn't so lackadaisical, as you do have a job to do in delivering mail, but I think a similar spirit is there.

When it comes to delivering mail, there is a Death Strandingian element to it in your need to place your boxes on your BMX (which you can do sick tricks and flips on, of course) to maximise how much you can deliver. A bit less stressful than Kojima's joint, obviously, though elements are still there. Any money you earn from this gig can then be spent on restoring the shrine that you oh so love, which falls onto the sim side of things with the ability to fully customise how the shrine looks.

There are also a whole heap of minigames to perform that helps you get to know the locals. I'm talking baseball, sumo wrestling, working in a sushi restaurant and, of course, fishing. You can see bits of that in the launch trailer above, which comes with as 2010s an anime opening song you could wish for with some animation so good it makes me want an adaptation of the game. In time, perhaps! You can pick it up on Steam right here.

Some spoilers for A Dog’s Perfect Christmas can be found in this piece

Christmas movies have officially hit the 2026 TV Schedule and taken over my life. Between Hallmark’s Countdown to Christmas, Netflix, and even Hulu, the new Christmas movie options are endless. It can be hard to decide what to watch, and when I saw the trailer for Netflix’s A Dog’s Perfect Christmas, I knew it had to be moved to the top of my list, even if I was sure it was going to make me cry.

The book-to-screen adaptation centered on the Goss family during a difficult holiday season when Juliana (Kathleen Rose Perkins) fell ill, leaving her workaholic husband (Milo Ventimiglia) and depressed father-in-law (Dennis Quaid) in charge of their teenage daughter (Brooke Lena Johnson), rambunctious twins, and beloved basset hound. The film was largely narrated by Winstead the beloved basset hound, and also included an adorable corgi puppy that Ello, the teenage daughter, rescued from the streets.

A Dog’s Perfect Christmas had something for everyone: adorable dogs, family drama, and even romance. I knew it was going to be an emotional watch from the start, but I couldn’t have imagined what led me to reach for the tissues over and over again.

I don’t think I’m the only one who immediately worries for a dog’s safety when they’re in a movie. Hollywood has a long history of killing beloved family dogs, so much so that there are entire websites dedicated to finding out if a movie contains a pet death. I’m someone who doesn’t like spoilers, though, so I’ve always refrained from checking it out, which is why I spent a large chunk of A Dog’s Perfect Christmas terrified for Winstead.

The odds were stacked against Winstead from the start. He was old, his human was already depressed about losing his wife, and the teenage daughter had brought a new puppy into the home. Plus, Winstead made it clear that his goal was to make his human (Quaid) find happiness again. The closer he got to that goal, the more I started to worry for his fate.

Thankfully, Winstead was spared from a tragic Hollywood ending, and so was Ruby, the adorable corgi puppy who officially becomes a member of the family by the end.

Netflix spared me from sobbing over a dead dog, but I still shed several tears while watching A Dog’s Perfect Christmas. Watching the family have to deal with Juliana’s illness was heartbreaking, especially knowing that they had already gone through a huge loss a couple of years prior. I couldn’t help but get teary-eyed when Hunter and Sander had to sit Ello down and explain how sick her mom really was.

While there were plenty of sad tears shed over the course of the film, there were also several times I found myself crying because I was laughing so hard. That was all thanks to Winstead. Even though the dog didn’t die, I still ended up shedding a few years about him anyway.

As the trailer suggested, Winstead was the pseudo-narrator of the film, introducing audiences to the Goss family and keeping us up to date. Of course, he did all this from his dog perspective, which led to some hilarious and touching moments. For example, he referred to Juliana as Juliana-Mom since that’s what he heard everyone calling her, and Christmas became “Merry Christmastime.”

The moments that made me cry from laughter, though, were anytime Winstead intervened to try and bring the family together, but ended up making a mess instead. He yanked a tablecloth off to get Sander and Ello to help each other clean up, and he regularly got the twins hyper in the hopes of making Sander smile.

Any dog owner will recognize the look of a dog who thinks they’re helping but is actually making things worse, and that’s exactly what Winstead did time and time again. I also couldn’t help but get teary-eyed from laughter every time Winstead judged Ruby for making a puppy mistake.

Before you return to the classics and watch one of the best Christmas movies of all time, check out A Dog’s Perfect Christmas, streaming now for everyone with a Netflix subscription. And don’t forget to check out all the upcoming Christmas movies still coming this holiday season.

#3795. Following BioWare's shock closure, a new documentary capturing its final moments is coming next year

A documentary detailing the history of beloved Mass Effect studio BioWare is releasing next year, and will cover last month's shock closure of the studio, following the private acquisition of owner EA.

Mass Effect: The BioWare Story (per Deadline) has been written and directed by Akash Sherman and produced for Canada's Super Channel. It documents the studio from the early days after its founding in 1995 to the release of barn-burner hits like Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Filming began two years prior to the announcement of BioWare's closure and continued throughout, with Deadline reporting the documentary will "capture BioWare’s final chapter."

The BioWare Story includes interviews with studio founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk, and Augustine Yip, alongside Mass Effect director Casey Hudson, other BioWare developers, and Shepard voice actor Jennifer Hale. That's alongside former EA CEO John Riccitiello, LucasFilm Games vice president Douglas Reilly, and creator of The Game Awards Geoff Keighley.

"The BioWare founders are my hometown heroes,” writer and director Sherman said in a statement accompanying the documentary news. "It's a privilege and responsibility to share the journey of underdogs who came together to create deeply beloved storytelling. Their golden era kindled a spark in me and in an entire generation. With the studio's recent closure, the film is now a profound valediction."

For fans outside Canada, Mass Effect: The BioWare Story is planned for a major film festival run and a world premiere next year. No exact release date has been established as of writing.

Members of the games industry have lambasted EA's decision to close Bioware in the weeks since the news was shared, with legendary designer Warren Spector writing, "Anyone who participated in this travesty should be ashamed". Meanwhile, a petition has reached enough signatures for the Canadian government to potentially rescue the studio from closure. Whether or not it actually does… Well, weirder things have happened?

Developer of entertainment products and pillar of the global economy Rockstar has announced that Grand Theft Auto 6, its much-ballyhooed upcoming Bonnie and Clyde simulator, will be targeting 30 frames per second on consoles. Coincidentally, "on consoles" is the only place Rockstar has currently announced the game is releasing, so GTA 6 is a 30-fps-or-bust experience for the foreseeable future.

"Grand Theft Auto 6 has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life", say the boys and girls in Edinburgh, while offering a little sweet treat to PlayStation 5 Pro owners in the form of PSSR (PlayStation of Soviet Socialist Republics—no, wait, sorry, PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution) support and ray-traced shadows.

Why am I telling you this on PC Gamer dot com? Partially because the traffic gods would beat me with a roll of pennies in a sock if I passed up an opportunity to write about GTA 6, but mostly because I'm very smug, and wish to subject other people to that.

Let's be real, the odds that GTA 6 was gonna target 60 fps on the box you have under your TV were always slim to none, but hearing it makes me feel more vindicated in my choice to wait for the game to hit PC than ever. I'm sure Rockstar's tech magi will make it a very nice 30 fps indeed, but my TV has 120 hertz in it. My monitor? 144, which I gather is kind of on the low end these days.

When it comes time for me to luxuriate in the lights of Leonida, I want to do it with maximum butteriness, I want all the bells and whistles set to 'on', and I want to do it on a proper gaming platform (German Linux). I'm excited to hear people's reports about what this game's actually like when it finally hits consoles in just over a week, but personally? I've never been happier about my choice to wait for GTA 6's inevitable but unannounced PC port.

#3793. Square Enix accidentally botches a Nier: Automata update, balloons required file size from 50GB to 366GB on PC

"Do you think games are silly little things?"

Yesterday, Nier: Automata received a new patch on Steam, adding more language support to the title - it can now be played with Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese options - but this new update also, somehow, inflated the file size of the game on PC from about 50GB to 366GB. D'oh! What's worse is, the update is not optional.

The cause of this, reportedly, is a bug that caused all the DLC in the YoRHa Edition of the game to become the same size as the base game - and the new download stacks them all concurrently. "Only SquareEnix can turn 40GB into 366GB with 8GB patch," says one dissatisfied Steam reviewer.

If you don't have space for this massive new file on your PC (and I can't say I blame you, it's ridiculous), there is a workaround, as confirmed by Square Enix in a tweet via its Japanese Twitter account.

"We have confirmed an issue where, following the latest update to the Steam version of Nier: Automata, the installation process indicates that more storage space is required than expected," noted the publisher. "We are currently investigating the cause and working on a solution. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. As a temporary workaround, you can download the base game by unchecking the DLC under Steam → Properties → DLC."

It's quite ironic, really, that so many Steam reviewers are complaining about things like "I just need to delete 90% of my computer to install this" when a large part of the game is managing the software/programmes installed on your android protagonists in order to upgrade your abilities and stats. There's even an ending for uninstalling your OS on your mechanical main characters. I'd be inclined to suggest this is some sort of meta psy-op from creator Yoko Taro, but… nah, that's just fantasy, isn't it? Isn't it?

Speaking of Taro, earlier this year we learned that "Nier Automata will continue", though we only heard back in 2025 that most of the projects the developer was working on were cancelled. One of these may have been the Tencent-backed Nier mobile game in 2024, which reportedly "struggled to find a monetisation to offset its high costs."

How Atlus veteran Kouji Okada shaped his next RPG

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Persona series casts a heck of a shadow, so founding Atlus member Kouji "Cozy" Okada, widely known as a godfather to Shin Megami Tensei and branching series including Persona, accepts that his new game, Villion:Code, a school-set action RPG with genome editing baked into its DNA, is going to invite some comparisons. Speaking with GamesRadar+ in a new video interview, Okada says Persona definitely has definitely influenced his work, but so have the many, many other games he's worked on and created.

Before a period of mobile-focused game development, Okada had been making RPGs since the 1980s, dating back to the original Megami Tensei, leading into Persona precursor Shin Megami Tensei If..., and covering the original three Persona games themselves. You don't just shrug off that kind of experience for the sake of being arbitrarily different.

"There is no doubt that Persona influenced this title," Okada says of Villion:Code, which is out January 26, 2027 on PS4, PS5, Switch, Switch 2, and Steam. "However, the same can be said of the many other series and standalone games I have worked on throughout my career."

We asked Okada if Persona and Shin Megami Tensei directly influenced his approach to Villion:Code, or if all of these games sit in the same place in his mind. "That is quite a perceptive question," he responds, saying it touches on his overall approach to games.

"This may stray slightly from the question, but although I would not go so far as to call it my personal philosophy, I believe games stand apart from other forms of entertainment because they make the fullest use of interactivity," he explains.

"Players provide input through a controller, for example, and their actions directly change what happens within the game. To make the most of that interactivity, I have always been particular about placing the player in the role of the protagonist, both in my previous titles and in Villion:Code. By asking, 'What would you do?' and allowing the player's decisions and actions to shape what unfolds, I hope to present players with a variety of questions and messages through the experience."

Comparisons to Persona don't necessarily bother Okada, but he stresses the differences between his previous works and Villion:Code. Its action combat system and unusual, tubular, almost vein-like dungeon design immediately stand out.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

"There is no doubt that Persona, through both its setting and its overall approach, helped us reach a much broader audience," he recalls. "Villion:Code also ultimately takes place in a school setting. When considering how to create a similarly intimate setting, [we] felt that a familiar, relatable world would work best. We wanted longtime players who had followed my previous work to enjoy it, but as I mentioned earlier, I also especially wanted younger players to experience the game. I hoped to convey a variety of messages through its story and other elements, which is why we chose a school setting.

"That said, our intention was not to create a different version of Persona. The setting was chosen solely because we felt it would communicate the world of Villion:Code most clearly. I understand that players may have their own impressions and comparisons, but personally, I regard the two as fundamentally separate works."

Atlus, meanwhile, is very loudly trying to create new Personas – specifically Persona 6, which will follow the series' latest remake, Persona 4 Revival.

#3791. World of Warcraft: Forever hotfix puts a stop to super speedy flag carriers that were dominating PvP battlegrounds

World of Warcraft: Forever has received its first major hotfix patch, which among other things has put an end to an especially powerful bug that made PvP battlegrounds like Warsong Gulch favoured to the Horde's advantage.

While Taurens are running, they gradually build up stacks of increased movement speed. They gain a two percent movement speed bonus per stack, and it stacks up to 30 times. That means a Tauren can gain 60 percent increased movement speed, though it's worth noting that when they stop moving, these stacks decrease. In short, cows run fast.

The Hotfix, detailed in this Blizzard blog post, stops the Tauren's plainsrunning passive from stacking during a battleground's preparation phase. What players were doing to exploit this was running back and forth in the minutes before the Warsong Gulch battleground let both teams loose. It's a capture the flag game mode, so once the gates opened, Taurens were sprinting ahead of everyone else, allowing them to quickly push towards the enemy base for a potential early flag capture.

In addition, the hotfix removes any plainsrunning stacks from Taurens once they pick up the enemy flag, and prevents them from gaining stacks while the flag is in their possession. The goal of the enemy team is to stop and kill the enemy flag carrier as soon as possible, so a Tauren moving far faster than any of your team made this pretty difficult.

Tauren's could be tanky warriors or druids too, which further added to the difficulty in killing them. With this change they're now easier to lock down, though it's worth noting a Tauren can still make use of Plainsrunning to rush into the enemy base early. They just don't have that wild speed boost from the jump.

Surely this was the only reason my Alliance Warsong Gulch games were all lost this morning, and not because my faction is for chumps. In other World of Warcraft: Forever news, the launch earlier this week was applauded as one of the smoothest in the series history, save for a few broken boats and zeppelins.

The hotfix has also decreased the respawn time of the NPC Deathstalker Erland who is needed for an escort quest. People were mulling around his spawn and wasting away while waiting for him to respawn. Also, supply vendors on the Zephras Isle have been stocked with handy tradeskill bags that you could find in other starter zones. It's the shipping I assume, it takes a while for stock to make it all the way up there.

The customers didn't hold back their thoughts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Kim Kardashian is a bona fide billionaire, and that’s in great part due to the performance of her shapewear and clothing brand, SKIMS. The company has seen immense growth and success in recent years, though it now finds itself in a bit of hot water with customers. Just recently, SKIMS dropped its latest advent calendar, and buyers aren’t happy with the items included. The company has since vowed to provide refunds to those who purchased the item but, ahead of that, many took to the Internet to roast this new product from “Kimberly.”

SKIMS has dropped more than a few items over the years that have prompted consumers to splurge, from its signature nipple bras to the more recent “micro fits.” Advent calendars have also been commonly offered by the brand though, and this latest one costs $148. With that price point, buyers were upset to discover that the calendar only included common items like SKIMS-branded bobby pins, hair clips and a small bear keychain. One X user reposted a product review from TikTok, and many users took to the comment section to weigh in:

Comments like these haven’t been limited to X, as some people have also posted about the product on Instagram since its release in early November. One user shared a photo of the calendar and the products and expressed disappointment via their caption:

A post shared by Marina Kelawon (@anthophilic.mermaid)

As mentioned before, though, SKIMS has responded to the situation, as the company shared a statement with Today, saying that it was “aware of the feedback.” The spokesperson confirmed the brand’s intention to provide refunds to dissatisfied customers and also said the following:

We have personally contacted every customer who purchased the calendar and offered them a choice of a full refund or a SKIMS credit to put towards other products. We want every customer to be truly happy with what they receive from SKIMS. Their feedback matters to us and will directly shape how we approach future releases.

This isn’t the first time that SKIMS has been on the receiving end of negatively charged publicity. In 2022, the company received blowback due to a controversy revolving around Kim Kardashian being edited in an ad. 2024 also saw fans outraged due to Kardashian and co. releasing boxers, which many compared to postpartum hospital diapers. A number of people also doubted whether Kardashian was actually modeling the XS size in advertisement materials.

It can’t be said with certainty just how many advent calendars SKIMS has sold this year but, regardless, the company now finds itself in a position to provide some reimbursement. Something that remains unclear at this point, though, is whether Kim Kardashian and her collaborators will choose to make changes to the existing calendar or take this feedback and apply it to the one for next year.

#3789. You can now buy GTA 6’s Grotti Cheetah sports car in real life, but the price tag fits its ridiculousness

If you’ve ever wanted to own a Grand Theft Auto car in real life, now is your chance.

In partnership with West Coast Customs (remember Pimp My Ride?) for the anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto 6, Rockstar Games has brought the legendary Grotti Cheetah sports car into the real world. And you’ll only need about £1 million to pick it up. That’s about $1,344,250 in US dollars, by the way.

Here’s your chance to own a part of automotive & gaming history! We’re incredibly proud to have partnered with Rockstar Games® to bring the custom in-game Grotti Cheetah from ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ to life. See the full details: https://t.co/kakQSnoh96 pic.twitter.com/2CkYUtjEqF

“Few cars epitomize GTA quite like the Grotti Cheetah,” said the car’s listing on the website for Selfridges, a UK-based retail chain that’s selling the one of a kind vehicle. “For the launch of GTA 6, Rockstar Games collaborated with West Coast Customs to bring an icon to The Corner Shop. Painted in Vice City’s signature pink and blue hues, this customized retro sports car is available to purchase for £1 million via Selfridges Personal Shopping.”

The listing then links to a contact page where only those with bank accounts way, way, WAY bigger than mine will be taken seriously when it comes to owning the one-of-one recreation.

I can’t even fathom what happens when it comes to buying something like this. Do they just take the first offer, or do they go for the best offer available? Why is it not going to auction? Either way, the car looks totally bad-ass with a sort of ombre of baby blue into hot pink, evoking Vice City’s aesthetic.

What say you, dear reader? Will you be picking up this car for your own garage (I’m assuming you own more than one vehicle, if so)? And if so, can I have a loan? GTA 6 finally launches next week, so I’ll be focusing my time there rather than a different kind of fantasyland where I could remotely entertain the idea of affording a car like this.

#3788. Bringing Bloodborne back is tricky because "there's a lot of involved rights associated," according to former PlayStation boss

Every year, Bloodborne fans pray for the birth of another game set in FromSoftware's Lovecraftian world. Every year, we're no closer to a Bloodborne 2 or even a Bloodborne Remastered. But why? PlayStation's former head honcho, Shawn Layden, blames it on the tricky situation of rights ownership.

Asked about the noticeable lack of Bloodborne in the decade since its blood moon shone down on us all, in an interview with The Trophy Room podcast, Layden explained that returning to any beloved game is tough.

"Bringing back old games has a certain challenge to it," he said. "Can you do something that is not only respectful of the original, but can you, you know, recreate the phenomenon as it were?"

Bloodborne's situation is slightly more complicated, though. It seems that the rights are somehow split between original publisher PlayStation, developer FromSoftware and the studio's primary stakeholder Kadokawa Corporation.

"There's a lot of involved rights associated with it, and in something like that - where Sony's in there and [FromSoftware] is in there and From's parent company is in there - I think just getting everyone to sign off on the same thing is probably the biggest challenge there," Layden said.

Having led the PlayStation brand during most of its PS4 golden years, Layden said working with FromSoftware on Bloodborne and the original Demon's Souls was "fantastic."

Despite endless calls for a comeback and very stable sales more than a decade on, Bloodborne itself is still stuck on the PS4 - though it's still playable via backward compatibility on the PS5, I should add. The closest we seemingly got to a Bloodborne comeback came from Bluepoint Games, which reportedly pitched a remake sometime before parent company PlayStation shut down the acclaimed studio, though FromSoftware supposedly didn't want the project to go ahead.

Another former PlayStation executive, Shuhei Yoshida, previously speculated that Bloodborne hasn't been remade because game director and soulslike pioneer, Hidetaka Miyazaki, would prefer to handle it himself: "Miyazaki-san really, really loved Bloodborne, what he created… So I think he is interested but he's so successful and he's so busy, so he cannot do it himself, and he doesn't want anyone else to touch it."

Elsewhere, a Bloodborne animated feature is in the works with YouTuber JackSepticEye attached as a co-producer.

#3787. James Gunn’s brave and bold vision for the DCU deserved better than early grave

Is this the end of the DCU? Probably not, but it's a sad day all the same

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You'll have heard the news by now... As announced yesterday, James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping away from DC Studios to be replaced by former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham. The first phase of the DCU, it seems, is over. What comes next? Well, that's still very much TBC.

This is not entirely shocking news, but it’s still – for me at least – something of a downer. Gunn and Safran's DCU has been surprising, strange, daring, occasionally baffling, and often thrilling. I loved Superman and Lanterns and liked Peacemaker, Clayface, and Creature Commandos a great deal.

OK, the Supergirl film was a misfire and proved that Gunn's winning style was not so easily aped by other directors, but even that had its moments: Milly Alcock was terrific in the lead role, and Krypto is always fun.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe has been frequently criticised for the homogeneity of its output, but that was never a criticism that could be levelled at the DCU, which veered from family-friendly superhero flicks to rated-R horror movies with any given project.

That's probably not good news if you're a Warner Bros. exec desperately trying to forge the next big mega-franchise, however. And it's true that it has sometimes been hard to understand exactly what the criteria were for a DCU project making it to the screen or not. We exist in a strange timeline where we have a fairly solid Clayface movie, but no DCU Batman to go with it.

Still, when the DCU was good, it was great. Gunn's Superman managed the difficult task of delivering a fresh take on the Man of Steel. David Corenswet charmingly embodies Supes' decency, humor, and willingness to take a beating in a way that echoes Christopher Reeve's character-defining performance, but feels more in tune with the comics.

It helps that the supporting cast in that film – Rachel Brosnahan as Lois Lane, Edi Gathegi as Mister Terrific, and especially Nicholas Hoult as a scheming, raging Lex Luthor – were all pitch-perfect.

Then there was Lanterns. I will fully admit to being a die-hard fan of Damon Lindelof's work (The Leftovers is up there with the greatest shows of all time and I will never shut up about it) so I came to this with high expectations and was not let down.

Sure, some fans may have disagreed with the decision to squeeze the cosmic grandeur of the Green Lantern mythology into a self-consciously "grounded" cop show format, but it worked – and then some. Kyle Chandler's spiky, flawed Hal Jordan and Aaron Pierre's stoic, determined John Stewart were the dynamic duo we didn't know we needed, and their investigation into extraterrestrial weirdness in small-town America was both gripping and thought-provoking. This wasn't just a great comic book show, but excellent TV full stop.

As for the rest... I had a lot of fun with Clayface, a gloopy, gruesome, enjoyably schlocky horror that still found time for solid characterization. It's not the sort of film you can build a cinematic universe around, but that's OK. Peacemaker season 2, meanwhile, did not hit quite the same heights as that bolt-from-the-blue first run, but John Cena remains hilarious and heartbreaking in the role. I hope that the character isn't left stranded on Salvation for too long.

So what does a post-Gunn, post-Safran DCU look like? Obviously I'm purely speculating here, but I suspect this will be a case of Latcham refocusing the brand, rather than relaunching the entire universe for a third time. And no, I don't see Zack Snyder returning any time soon...

It doesn't take the World's Greatest Detective to figure out that we'll likely see a sharper focus on the A-list DC characters: Batman, Wonder Woman, and probably reinventions of Aquaman and the Flash at some point. I would hope that it doesn't mean the end of DC trying out interesting lower-budget experiments like Clayface, but I suspect the days of somewhat obscure-sounding TV spin-offs like the upcoming The People v. Gorilla Grodd are over.

The Superman movies will also surely continue, perhaps even with Gunn involved in a third instalment – while his departure letter talked of "trying" times behind-the-scenes, he notably did not close the door on working with DC again and has already referenced another, unnamed project in progress. Frankly, Latcham would be foolish to try and find someone else to steer that character when Gunn is right there.

James Gunn was working on Superman 3 and a Justice League team-up when he was ousted at DC

The biggest question, of course, is what becomes of the Dark Knight – and that does feel like a particularly tricky knot to undo. Matt Reeves' The Batman: Part II (which is set in a different "Elseworlds" continuity) was originally slated to come out in 2025, leaving the way clear for the introduction of a new DCU Batman in a film, helmed by Gunn, titled The Brave and the Bold.

Alas, The Batman: Part II suffered a series of major delays and is now eyeing a February 2028 slot, while the fate of The Brave and the Bold is unclear at this time. Ultimately, the DCU needs to find its Caped Crusader sooner rather than later, and you can be sure that figuring out how to introduce this new Batman, while also promoting Reeves' project, will be top of Latcham's to-do list at DC.

I'm not ready to write the future of the DCU off just yet, but I will miss the unpredictable energy that Gunn and Safran have brought to these movies and shows over the last four years. It's been a bumpy ride at times, but never a boring one, and I'd take a series with a strong authorial voice like this over a play-it-safe franchise any day.

Is that what we'll get with the DCU Chapter Two? Only time and a former Marvel exec named Jeremy Latcham will tell.

Clayface is in theaters now. The future may be in flux, but here's everything we know right now about DCU Chapter One and all the upcoming DC movies and shows.

#3786. A California airplane got evacuated when a passenger playing Call of Duty was overheard talking about a bomb

You can't just say "bomb" on an airplane.

There really is a proper time and place for things, gamers. Please know that when you’re taking your sweaty callouts into public places.

An avid Call of Duty player reportedly caused their plane to be evacuated last night after they were overheard making callouts, according to CBS News. The Frontier Airlines flight was preparing to take off from Ontario International Airport when a complaint was filed.

The complaint, from another passenger on board, said that they heard someone say words “bomb” and “explosion” and then reported it to the crew. The plane then had to be evacuated and the gamer in question was detained.

The CoD-head was ultimately detained and then had to explain to authorities that “bomb” and “explosion” were used to describe his gameplay, as he was playing the game while on FaceTime with a friend and making callouts mid-match.

I’m normally a big proponent of communication in online games, especially shooters like CoD where teamwork is paramount. Maybe just…not while on an airplane, huh? It’s unclear what CoD game the player was enjoying, but it could’ve been the new Modern Warfare 4 now that it’s portable and playable on the go with Nintendo Switch 2.

And when it comes for saying “bomb” on an airplane, it’s probably not the smartest idea. Traveling is stressful enough and people are on edge, so no matter how silly you may think the other passenger was being, I understand it. Plus, all I can really think of is this one scene from the Ben Stiller/Robert De Niro classic comedy, Meet the Parents:

CBS News said crews swept the plane and found no bomb or explosive device on board, thankfully. There was no word about whether or not the CoD player and his friend won the match in question, although I don’t think the rest of the people on that plane really cared.

#3785. Mass Effect-like RPG The Expanse: Osiris Reborn ropes in David Gaider, the original lead writer of Bioware's Dragon Age series

"Focusing on certain aspects of the game's narrative."

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn looks like it's carrying the best bits of Mass Effect forward, and in an encouraging move, the developers have been collaborating with David Gaider.

Of course, David Gaider is best known as the lead writer on Dragon Age: Origins, Dragon Age 2 and Dragon Age: Inquisition - he's also often credited as the architect of its dark fantasy world Thedas. Gaider's post-BioWare career saw him open his own game development house Summerfall Studios, which most recently released an ambitious roleplaying musical called Stray Gods.

But he's now lending a hand to a game that's not too dissimilar to BioWare's other hugely famous roleplaying series, while still working on his own games at Summerfall.

"Alongside my work at Summerfall, I've also been collaborating with the Owlcat Games team on The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, focusing on certain aspects of the game's narrative. The Expanse has long been one of my favourite series, and so obviously I jumped at the opportunity to be involved," he wrote on BlueSky.

"The Owlcat team has been so great, it's really such a treat. One thing I enjoy is how responsive they are to the fans," Gaider added, pointing to how the studio recently recast the male version of its protagonist in response to feedback. The game's reworked and re-designed Martian Captain is now voiced by Blythe Melin.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn shouldn't be confused for the other very Mass Effect-y RPG coming out next year, Exodus. Though it's good to hear that both upcoming projects have some BioWare veterans on board, especially after the famed developer was shut down and had its own promising, actual Mass Effect game cancelled.

Bertie enjoyed what he played of the upcoming game in Eurogamer's The Expanse preview, but also had some concerns about the developer's use of generative AI.

Finally, some answers about those Buzzes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Pixar movies have been entertaining audiences for decades, especially the Toy Story franchise. We were treated to another adventure with everyone's favorite toys when Toy Story 5 hit theaters earlier this year, with the project now streaming with a Disney+ subscription. I've been wondering why that army of Buzz Lightyears spent so much of the film wandering around the woods, and now we finally have some answers behind that narrative choice.

Toy Story 5 reviews were positive, and plenty of folks liked the running gag of all the Buzz Lightyears roaming around the woods together. During an interview with Gold Derby, director/writer Andrew Stanton got real about why the squad of Buzz toys spent so much time in the wilderness. As he explained:

We wanted them in the woods because then they wouldn't be constantly bumping into humans. And we just needed a nondescript shortcut to get wherever they're going. But then somebody in my story group drew a Buzz Lightyear petting a bunny, and it was like watching an actor choose something that was instinctual. We all knew that deep down under that tough exterior that Buzz has such a soft heart. And animals can sense when you're kind. And it just made sense that they would get along with cute woodland creatures.

Honestly, this makes a great deal of sense. We all know that toys in the animated franchise play dead whenever humans encounter them, hiding the secret that they're actually alive. So when Toy Story 5 brought in an entire group of new Buzz Lightyears, they had to be put in a setting that allowed the action figures to continue guarding that secret.

Toy Story 5 made fans appreciate Jessie, but the running gag of all the Buzz Lightyears was a delightful side plot during the movie's 102-minute runtime. It was heartwarming to see the toys connecting with various animals in the woods, which also served as an A+ reference to Bambi. As the filmmaker went on to share:

And there's something meta about woodland creatures and animation and Bambi, and it just felt like all these roads met at the same time to the degree that when we were putting the scene together and it was cracking us up privately by putting Bambi's ['Love Is a Song'] in there. I said we should look into getting the rights because it's the one time I would be willing to go off script composer-wise, much to Randy Newman's chagrin. But to really sell the joke and to sell the moment, it's just this kind of animation history.

The Toy Story franchise is known for including easter eggs to other Disney projects, so the fact that the fifth movie went full Bambi shouldn't have come as much of surprise. Still, I'm glad that we got some answers about why the Buzz squad was kept in the woods for the majority of the movie.

Toy Story 5 is streaming now on Disney+ as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll just have to see if the House of Mouse moves forward with a sixth installment of the beloved property.

#3783. Updated Xbox PC app promises 60% faster loading and easier access to games, but CEO Asha Sharma says there's "plenty more to do"

The Xbox PC app hasn't had the best track record in recent years, but Microsoft is promising that it's now much faster and easier to use than before.

Starting today, anyone part of the Xbox Insiders program can try out the new improvements. According to Microsoft, the updated Xbox PC app now boots up 60% faster, several pages can launch up to 50% faster, and in-app windows can open up to 65% faster. The company acknowledged that performance can vary based on your set up, internet connection, device, and so on.

The rest of the update involves "simpler navigation, updated filters, and new ways to organise your games," according to Xbox Wire, while social features are now included in the main navigation menu so you can start playing or chatting with friends quicker.

A faster Xbox PC app is certainly nice for players who regularly use it, though it's still missing a lot of the features that make Steam the go-to place to buy PC games. CEO Asha Sharma called the update "a meaningful improvement," but acknowledged there's still "plenty more to do."

Microsoft also said "it's easier to find what you're looking for" using the app's search function, and refreshed game cards and animations should give the platform "a cleaner look and feel."

Elsewhere, the revamped cloud gaming setup will roll out to even more people using web browsers, and more Xbox Insiders should hear about the program over the next few weeks. "The updated experience also makes it easier to find and play your games," the company said while bringing attention to its new light and dark modes. Supported smart TVs and VR headsets will get the updated cloud experience, as well.

Earlier this year, the console maker brought a selection of 'classic' games to PC for the first time ever - Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge and Fuzion Frenzy led the first batch. Mythic Achievements - the Platinum Trophy equivalent - went live for all Xbox players, too.

Those birds kept stealing all my good cards.

What's worse than fighting one human-sized bird with sunglasses? Fighting two human-sized birds with sunglasses. That wasn't a usual problem in my everyday life until I started playing Stack Order's demo, the hand-drawn deckbuilder that's full of duels and fantastic combos.

The run began with my masked character locked away in a jail cell, not all that dissimilar to how I start most of my days. However, this time I was promptly freed by a stranger who wanted to help out. After handing me a deck of cards and talking me through how to use it, I was left to go on my merry way. The only problem was that I didn't get very far before a knight called Robert, who was very unhappy to see me out of my cell, butted in.

I've played my fair share of deckbuilders so it wasn't exactly a steep learning curve. But unlike some other games, Stack Order puts a very strong emphasis on stacking cards. You need to lose the bad habit of just playing one card at a time and instead start stacking cards at the first chance you get.

But, crucially, stacking cards doesn't necessarily mean you have to use them, you could get everything ready and then forfeit your go or just use a throwaway attack. Most killing blows in Stack Order come down all at once after you've stacked several cards all with varying multipliers and unleash it all at once.

Certain cards, for example, deal extra damage if they come before or after cards, others add damage to specific cards if they're stacked below them. You get a random assortment of cards on each turn, so you can't always bet on a dream stack, but if you're smart you can usually create one hell of a combo.

The only problem is that you're not the only one who can pack a punch. Each enemy I came up against had their own set of skills which changed the fight. Knight Robert had a simple yet effective attack / block combo, the Queen slowly poisoned me, but the birds, those two damn birds really topped it all.

First off there were two of them, which meant extra attacks, but to make matters worse each bird had a special effect that would see them deal extra damage the more cards you left on the table and would steal either the top of bottom card of each stack and use it to buff themselves, including how much they were able to heal. This made things really tricky.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

I quickly found out that if I didn't kill them quickly we'd roll into a painfully long stalemate, as I would just barely hang on with shields and they were able to heal 11 damage every third turn. Damage them enough and you can break some of their attacks, they'll still deal damage but won't get the bonus perk.

Managing how you build stacks, when you can't build multiple and also need to leave a sacrifice card for one of the birds to eat, is taxing to be sure. But that's what makes winning fights in Stack Order all the more rewarding.

I managed to experience this euphoria after I bested the pair of birds, but that wasn't the last I'd see of them as, after dying to the next boss, I had to restart my run. Soon I was fighting Robert, the Queen, and the dastardly bird duo all over again, and let me tell you it does not get easier the second time you fight them.

#3780. Xbox is testing a way to use your phone as a controller on smart TVs

Xbox is testing two new ways to play its cloud games, and one of them doesn't require a controller at all.

Announced on Xbox Wire on 4th November, the phone controller preview is rolling out on supported TVs wherever Xbox Cloud Gaming is available. The phone option - which works with both Android and iOS devices - lets you use your phone "as a controller when you don't have one nearby". Connect to your TV via QR code, and the controls open in your phone's browser.

The second preview, called cloud connect, is currently limited to the US and lets the new Xbox Nano controller talk to your cloud session over wi- fi instead of pairing directly with your TV to "help reduce input latency, so gameplay feels more responsive".

To try out the phone controls yourself, switch on Preview Features under Settings > Account in the latest version of the Xbox smart TV app.

Xbox has published a setup guide with full instructions, although you should note that both experiences "are still being tested", so the availability and supported games or devices "may be limited while [Xbox] learns from your feedback".

ICYMI, as of yesterday, anyone in the Xbox Insider Program can try Microsoft's updated Xbox PC app. The company claims it now boots up 60% faster, several pages can launch up to 50 percent faster, and in-app windows can open up to 65 percent faster.

#3779. Complete DREADMOOR Walkthrough: Part 1

DREADMOOR is now out in early access, and it presents an interesting tale for you to explore. Set in a dark, murky world, you have to capture different fish, explore locations, and upgrade your boat.

The campaign of DREADMOOR begins with a tentacle knocking you in the water. The story is broken into multiple quests that you can complete.

The opening will lead you to safe piece of land, and your main objective to get your boat. To do so, you’ll have to power up the generator with the fuel. Once you reach the generator, go to the hut right from there. You’ll find the fuel to power up the generator.

Once the generator has been powered up, you’ll unlock the boat, and then start exploring the world of DREADMOOR. Make sure to pick up the Hook Gun as well along the way.

First, we have to head to the Church Settlement. This place will provide you with your first weapon that allows you to clear blockages. Moreover, you’ll also find the first bed where you can sleep for the night to be over.

Next, we set sail for the Trading Post. Here, we will meet the trader and he will task us with some quest. The trader will also provide us with different blueprints to purchase, but that’s something you can ignore for now.

From there, go upwards to patch the hole in the wall in your shelter. Here, you’ll find the Simple Rod, and you can now fish in the waters. But first, sleep on the bed to survive the night.

Once we get the fishing rod, the next task is to open the door to the Dry Dock. Get the required resources, and then speak with the Engineer to open the doors. This will then allow you to clean and upgrade your ship.

Before you can install the upgrades, you’ll also need to clean the polyps from your ship using the water pipe. Then, you can install the upgrades after crafting them with the required resources. To do so, you’ll have to unlock the blueprints first.

This will complete the first part of the game and get you up to date with all the basics.

Opinion | Please, Rockstar, join us in the light of 60 FPS

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 is targeting 30 FPS on PS5 and Xbox Series X. The same goes for the beefier PS5 Pro, which can now sit another exclusive on the shelf alongside Sony's marketing deal for the game: ray-traced shadows that have seen some people shell out $1,300. This is all fine and expected news, yet I'm saddled by the same tiny disappointment I feel every time a big console release targets 30 FPS.

It's not that I'll turn my nose at any game that isn't running at 60 FPS or higher, filthy PC gamer that I am. But if we're talking preferences, yeah, I do wish everything ran at 60 FPS at 1440p or below. I'd gladly accept lower graphical fidelity as a tradeoff for that and, more pertinently, I'll happily wait to play GTA 6 on PC if it means better performance.

This is easy for me to say, of course. I didn't have to move mountains to get a game of this scale running at 30 FPS to begin with. It might sound easy to put fidelity and frame rate on a scale and just subtract material until the FPS side rises, but I know it's not that simple, even if cuts could surely be made.

It's not just about the visible sweat, intricate clothing, innumerable environmental wrinkles, granular animations, or ray-traced shadows – all the little details that people at Rockstar have presumably achieved through blood sacrifice. This might actually be the best-looking game ever made by many metrics. But GTA 6 also has to handle dense NPC crowds, a sprawling city, seamless character switching, and all the unseen systems supporting that experience. That, to me, is the truly important, gameplay-affecting stuff.

I never care about graphics in any way that matters, and I always care about smoothness

It all amounts to more things for that frame rate to haul, and Rockstar seemingly chose 30 FPS with all the fixins' over higher FPS with all the sacrifices. I understand and respect that. Devs should make what they want, as ludicrously complex as they want it to be. But on that scale, my taste leans heavily toward frame rate for a few reasons.

Console generational leaps are getting smaller. This generation has, as far as I'm concerned, had only two real difference-makers: M.2 NVMe SSDs that dramatically improve loading times, and the spread of performance-focused graphic settings (or performance modes). As you may have guessed, I go for performance mode every single time.

Some games benefit more from having higher frame rates than others, but maximum FPS is always my pick until I hit 60. A fast-paced martial arts game like Phantom Blade Zero would be seriously hurt by a low or inconsistent frame rate, for instance. But I'm currently playing Persona 3 Reload, and its turn-based combat and simple environments aren't really bothered as long as the frame rate is half-decent and stable. But the choice is still simple: I never care about graphics in any way that matters, and I always care about smoothness. GTA 6 isn't a frenetic wuxia fiesta, but its driving and shooting definitely push it toward the more FPS-sensitive camp in my mind.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

There's a point where I lose interest in graphical improvements, and that point came at least 10 years ago. I can appreciate a cutting-edge game, whether it's GTA 6 NPCs whose calves flex with each step or a huge RPG like Cyberpunk 2077 with every setting cranked to the moon. But if AAA games eternally looked like late-gen PS4 releases, I honestly wouldn't complain. My threshold for game that looks good is comfortably below that, and an art style far removed from realism is more likely to grab me anyway. Now and forever, I'm more interested in games that run better and console gaming that feels, not necessarily looks, more like my PC experience (again, M.2s really helped with this). Hell, right now I just want consoles that people can actually afford, and pushing hardware to fruitlessly advance graphics won't get us those.

Every generation, I think these will surely be the systems to normalize 60 FPS, and I'm consistently let down by games going in the opposite direction for visuals that don't, and will never, move me. In all graphical discussions, my mind goes to an early Uncharted: Drake's Fortune demo showing how water would convincingly dampen Nathan Drake's clothes and then dry in the sun. Nearly 20 years later, it feels like we are still hung up on the equivalent of Nathan Drake getting wet even though this detail didn't mean squat to the experience of Uncharted and this kind of thing is infinitely less novel and relevant today. The real or imagined title of 'best-looking game ever made' has never meant less, and a significantly uglier version of GTA 6 would still assuredly blow my socks off. I'll tell you what would really impress me: a promise that this runs at twice the frame rate of GTA 5, a 13-year-old game.

#3777. Wardogs Season 3 brings an urban map, Limited Mode, and a 185,000-account ban wave

Wardogs' Season 3 will launch on 12th November, complete with a new urban map, a new Limited Mode, and a ban wave targeting 185,000 accounts.

Developer Bulkhead confirmed the details earlier this week, revealing plans for a full wipe and progression changes that it hopes will "recapture the shared discovery and sense of achievement that defined" the 100-player tactical shooter when it first launched in Early Access.

The new map will focus on close-quarters fighting, and for a "more level playing field", players can dip into Limited Mode, which offers "an alternative way to experience" the game as it restricts weapons, ammunition, armour, and vehicles.

While the full list of restrictions is still being decided, it currently includes FMJ-only ammunition, a Tier 2 armour cap, and a reduced attack vehicle selection.

"The mode is designed to preserve the feel of early-to-mid-game combat and reduce the advantage offered by more powerful equipment," the team said.

Bulkhead also confirmed seasons are getting longer. From now on, they’ll last three months, giving players "more time to work towards their goals before each wipe and the development team more time to prepare future updates". Progression will also be "brought closer to the pace of Season 1", following the studio’s acknowledgement that Season 2 accelerated "the journey too aggressively".

"Season 3 is about giving players a new battlefield to learn together and a progression journey worth spending time on," said Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer. "Longer seasons give everyone more room to reach their own goals, and give us the time to properly develop what comes next."

Alongside Season 3, Bulkhead revealed it has used machine learning to review is "activating further layers of its anti-cheat" after analysing 187 million hours of gameplay with help from machine learning. It says having close to four million unique players since launch gave it enough data to pull that work forward from next year.

"[E]xploiters, real-money traders, and gold-farming networks" have been permanently banned and lost their server-hosting privileges, and a player trust score is planned for 2027.

"Protecting the people who play Wardogs fairly is essential to everything we're building," Brammer added.

Bigger changes to the metagame, including a new progression system, are also due in 2027 as Bulkhead works towards Wardogs 1.0. Full Season 3 patch notes will be out before launch.

Wardogs launched in Steam Early Access on 10th September, and is due on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in 2028.

Wardogs is one of the breakout successes of the year. In our early access Wardogs review, we said the game's mix of competitive shooters' best bits with something entirely of its own made it "a brilliantly refreshing take on the genre".

Since Sir Patrick Stewart’s passing, I have spent a great deal of time reading stories from his co-stars about his work and impact. It’s lovely to see tributes continue to pour in, but the sentiments that have truly hit me in my feels have come from Ian McKellen, Stewart's longtime best friend (and sometimes on-screen nemesis). While Sir McKellen broke his silence weeks ago, he just shared additional thoughts on his late comrade, and I may or may not need a tissue.

While Stewart and McKellen battled on the big screen as X-Men's Professor X and Magneto, respectively, the two seem inseparable in real life. They were actually so close that McKellen even officiated Stewart’s wedding to Sunny Ozell in 2013. So, when the actor stopped by Entertainment Tonight to promote his movie, Ebenezer, he got a chance to reflect on his friendship with Stewart, and his comments are just too sweet:

Well, what I thought about Sir Patrick of late is because he did his own version of Christmas Carol. He was a one-man show. He played all the characters. He did it on Broadway and did it on London’s West End a number of times. I think he toured with it. It’s a big part of his life. I just remember his friendship and his - A good man. Serious-minded. And always looking to make the world a better place, and he achieved that.

I think everyone would be better off having a friend who speaks about them as lovingly as McKellen discusses Stewart. To put it simply, the two were the definition of friendship goals, and the seasoned actors elevated everyone around them. I can't imagine it's easy for McKellen not having his good friend around, but I love that he's choosing to remember him in such a positive way.

Of course, given McKellen’s role in Ebezener as Jacob Marley, it makes sense that his friend would be on his mind. Stewart's take on A Christmas Carol still serves as a high point in his career and a benchmark for stage acting in general. It seems I'm not the only one who is feeling a a way about this tribute either based on the comments of the Instagram video. I think toriyikes sums it best: “Making me cry in the afternoon!” Fans may agree after watch ingthe video below:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

Shortly after Patrick Stewart's death was reported, Ian McKellen took to X to share a sentimental message. In it, the star reflected on his and Stewart's time serving at the Royal Shakespeare Company and discussed their subsequent work and endearing friendship.

While Stewart was greatly known for his work as an actor, McKellen’s words were a a sweet reminder that he was so much more. Yes, he was “serious-minded,” but he was also always up for a laugh and even gave his own eulogy back in 2015 at a Just for Laughs gala. There's a reason his roles as Professor X and Jean-Luc Picard are still iconic, and it's because the compassion that he put into the world. Just as McKellen said, he made it a little better, and that's something we should all remember.

Of course, it should be noted that we will the two X-Men alums together one more time when Avengers: Doomsday hits the 2026 schedule on December 18. The movie will now mark Stewart's final on-screen performance following his death at 86 due to Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. Trailers have already teased that Stewart's Professor X and McKellen's Magneto will share the screen again, and I'm not sure I'm prepared for that reunion.

I'm confident that Patrick Stewart's final turn as the X-Men's leader will be satisfying and that his body of work as a whole will stand the test of time. More than that, though, if the comments from Ian McKellen and so many others are anything to go by, Stewart's kind spirit won't be forgotten either.

#3774. Assassin's Creed is reportedly going to ancient Rome, while a mobile spin-off heads to Jerusalem

Ubisoft is reportedly working on two new Assassin's Creed games, and one of them is set in ancient Rome.

That's according to YouTuber Xj0nathan, who says the Rome game is codenamed Mars. He claims two sources with access to Ubisoft's backend systems backed up the information, and that the setting will likely be linked to the upcoming Assassin's Creed TV series.

The second game, codenamed Pocket, is said to be a mobile title set in Jerusalem. Xj0nathan claims it'll play a bit like Assassin’s Creed Valhalla’s Mastery Challenge, and look similar to the most recent Prince of Persia. The hero's mentor is apparently a character called Myriam.

If Mars does move into full production, don't hold your breath - Insider Gaming doesn't expect us to hear anything about it until 2029 or 2030.

Assassin's Creed has visited Rome before, in 2010’s Brotherhood, but that was the Renaissance version of the city.

The leak comes less than a week after Ubisoft issued a statement about the future of the Assassin's Creed series, insisting there are currently no new remakes of the series' past games in the works.

#3773. How to check how many chests you’ve opened in Fortnite Treasure Hunters

Looting is more important than ever before in Fortnite’s Treasure Hunters mini-season, as there are lots of freebies up for grabs this time around, including access to everything in the shop if you get really lucky. Because of this, you may be searching for a way to keep track of how many chests you’ve opened.

Finding and opening chests is the only way to get your hands on quite a few rare items this season, so keeping an eye on all of the work you’ve put in is a helpful tool for tracking progress. It can be tricky to find on your own, though, so here’s how to check how many chests you’ve opened in Fortnite.

You can keep track of how many chests you’ve opened in Fortnite Treasure Hunters from the Quests tab. This helpful mechanic can be easy to miss, as there are quite a lot of missions to tackle listed in this section. Here’s how to find it.

Each of the chest quests listed here tracks your progress across five stages. As you hit each of the five milestones for these bonus goals, you earn extra XP, and the listed maximum number of chests being tracked increases.

These missions only track chests up to 1,000 for each type, so once you hit this number in each of the three categories, your total opened chests will no longer be displayed. This means you can only check your opened chests for the season up until you hit this cap.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

The number of chests you open does not directly affect your odds of finding the Pirate Shop Access or other special loot drop items. The loot odds and drop rates are completely unrelated to how many chests you open, as this system is completely based on RNG, which means it comes down to random luck and chance.

Although opening more chests doesn’t directly increase your odds of finding Pirate Shop Access and other loot items, the more you loot, the more shots you have at potentially finding something. This system can be a bit confusing to fully understand, but a good way to conceptualize it is to compare the loot system to a bag of marbles.

Think of all the special loot items as rare, colored marbles in a big bag of grey ones. Each time you open a chest, you’re pulling a marble out. If the marble is grey, it goes right back in. If it’s colored, it stays out.

Your odds of pulling a colored one, which is a special loot item, don’t increase over time, as the grey marbles, or standard loot items, always go back into the pool. At the same time, the more you reach into the bag by opening chests, the more shots you have at finding items.

Although you can’t boost your odds of finding rare drops by opening more chests, you can help the process along by attending special events that feature boosted odds for these rare items. Treasure Hours are the best time to go looting for these assets.

When it comes to monitors, Alienware increasingly has a habit of undercutting the competition. The new Alienware AW3226Q is no exception, offering LG's stunning new 4K RGB-stripe Tandem OLED panel for by far the lowest price yet.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

You know Alienware's 5K2K 39-inch ultrawide OLED gaming monitor beast, the AW3926QW, the one I reviewed the other day? It's an absolute beauty, probably my favourite current PC monitor, save for one niggly flaw. But what if you fancy something similar, but cheaper and in a more conventional 32-inch 4K form factor? Well, give it up for the new Alienware AW3226Q, because it ticks all those boxes.

Notably, it sports exactly the same LG Tandem WOLED panel tech as its bigger 39-inch sibling. That includes being the latest RGB-stripe variant of that new LG OLED panel generation that everyone is going bananas for.

Well, it's nearly the same. For reasons that aren't entirely clear, this 32-inch 4K panel clocks in at 250 nits full-screen brightness and 1,000 nits peak HDR. The aforementioned 39 incher rocks 300 nits and 1,300 nits figures for the same metrics, respectively.

250 nits full screen, 1,000 nits peak HDR

LG Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, 2x HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, USB-A/C hub, 3.5mm audio

✅ You're an OLED purist: LG's new RGB-stripe WOLED tech offers beautifully neutral colours.

❌ You want the brightest possible OLED experience: This version of LG's Tandem WOLED panel technology takes a small brightness hit.

As it happens, the numbers for this 32-inch 4K model are actually more in line with expectations for this panel type. The thing is, with all previous WOLED panel generations, LG used a white subpixel to boost brightness.

This new pure RGB-stripe—or red, green, blue—item ditches the white subpixel in favour of pixel precision and improved colour volume. But that comes with a cost in terms of peak brightness.

Even the 39-inch AW3926QW is a little dimmer than the RGWB version of LG's latest Tandem OLED monitor panel tech, where the "W" in "RGWB" indicates the added white subpixel. Oh, and just for clarity, the "W" in "WOLED" has always referred to the white colour of the light produced by the emissive OLED material in all of the subpixels, rather than the added white subpixels in all previous WOLED monitor generations prior to the newest RGB-stripe variants. Baffling, but there you go.

Anywho, monitors with RGWB Tandem OLED panels, including the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS I reviewed recently, tend to weigh in around 330 nits full-screen and 1,500 nits peak HDR. So the 39-inch 5K2K RGB-stripe panel gives less away in terms of brightness than expected, and in turn this new 32-inch 4K model is pretty much where you'd expect it to be.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Got all that? Then it's also worth understanding that those brightness figures can be misleading. Like I said, LG has been including a fourth white subpixel in all of its previous WOLED monitor panel generations to boost brightness. But that doesn't automatically boost colour brightness. At least it can't while maintaining colour volume.

That's why Samsung's competing QD-OLED panels, as also used by a wide variety of monitor makers including Alienware, have often looked more vibrant despite typically offering slightly lower ratings. Samsung has never used an additional white subpixel, so its brightness rating reflects real-world usage. And real-world gaming means a colour image rather than a pure white image pretty much all the time.

The point I'm making here is that it's important not to assume that the 4K RGB-stripe Tandem WOLED panel in this new Alienware is a step backwards just because it has lower brightness ratings than RGWB Tandem WOLED in monitors like that Asus model I mentioned above. It's more complicated than that.

Along with the brightness and colour volume implications, the RGB-stripe has the same pixel precision and text quality upsides here as it does on other RGB-stripe OLEDs. In short, the Windows OS assumes it is rendering to a conventional RGB-stripe subpixel layout, so having RGB-stripe solves issues like fuzzy text and colour fringing.

It's important not to assume that the 4K RGB-stripe Tandem WOLED panel in this new Alienware is a step backwards just because it has lower brightness ratings.

As for the rest of the speeds and feeds, well, the refresh is a relatively modest 165 Hz, the panel is flat, and it's covered in a glossy glare coating. Inputs include DisplayPort 1.4 and two HDMI 2.1 ports, but there's no USB-C for single-cable connectivity, albeit along with the two USB-A data ports, there is a USB–C downstream socket as part of the USB hub.

Oh, and I haven't mentioned the price. It's $699 or £649 at launch, which is pretty punchy, especially given the cutting-edge panel tech. Heck, the 34-inch ultrawide AW3426DW is more expensive. It's also not far off half the price of the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM, which has the same RGB-stripe panel, albeit running at a higher refresh and with more features.

So, the surprisingly low price perhaps explains the 165 Hz as opposed to 240 Hz refresh and lack of USB-C support. It's probably also why there's no dual-mode support offering a higher refresh rate at a lower resolution.

If that's the stats and specs covered, what's the actual gaming experience like? Mostly pretty fantastic. Like the bigger AW3926QW, I really like the AW3226Q's overall look and colour balance. It fixes the slightly washed out and green-tinted vibe of LG's RGWB panels without suffering from the overly warm colour temperature and purple-tint in bright ambient light of competing Samsung QD-OLED-based monitors.

In many ways, this is the perfect OLED panel tech, it's just so nice. The colours look super natural, the lighting control is perfect, and the response is basically instant. The 4K resolution on a 32-inch panel also makes for razor-sharp detail. It's pretty much the definitive modern PC gaming experience.

OKay, the 165 Hz refresh is a touch pedestrian these days, but this isn't an esports model and it's definitely a compromise built out of chasing affordability. And even with an RTX 5090, you're not going to be playing many modern games at 4K at 200fps-plus, in reality.

It's pretty much the definitive modern PC gaming experience.

The arguable exception to all that is full-screen brightness, which is just a touch disappointing. A lot of the time you won't notice it. On the Windows desktop if you enable dark mode and you haven't got a very bright browser or app window open, this monitor looks really punchy and vibrant.

The same goes for most game scenes with HDR enabled. They look absolutely stellar, with both bright and dark image elements precisely controlled in the same image. That's OLED per-pixel lighting for you, there's nothing quite like it. As ever, of course, the sizzle of small HDR highlights like light sources, sparks and explosions are a sight to behold.

Where this RGB-stripe 32 incher isn't quite so impressive is brighter outdoor game scenes. Here, it can look just a bit dull, with that 250 nit full-screen capability holding it back. To an extent, the 39-inch 5K2K model has the same problem. But it's that little bit brighter. We're talking fine margins, but where the 39 incher mostly seems to be just punchy enough, this 32-inch sibling just falls short of being enjoyably vibrant that little bit more often.

That said, Alienware has included a range of HDR modes, including standard HDR 400 and HDR 1000 models, plus an HDR 1000 Bright mode. The latter is supposed to offer the best of the other two modes in a single setting and from a subjective experience perspective, it largely does just that, offering the best this panel can achieve in terms of both full-screen brightness and peak HDR performance for small, super-bright highlights.

I'm pretty confident you can consider vignette dimming a solved problem.

So, what about that niggle I mentioned up front? With the 39-inch Alienware AW3926QW, I was disappointed to confirm that community reports of so-called "vignette dimming" were accurate. Long story short, Alienware had implemented an OLED protection feature known as CPC or Convex Power Control that slightly dims the edge of the panel when gameplay is detected.

The idea is to prevent static game interface elements like mini maps or health bars from causing burn-in. The problem was that Alienware didn't provide a toggle for CPC. It was always enabled. And all of that is also true for the new 32-inch Alienware AW3226Q.

At least it was. On November 5th, Alienware released a new firmware update for the 39-inch Alienware AW3926QW which includes a toggle for CPC, though it's called "Edge-Dimming" in the OSD. I haven't tested it myself, but it's reported to remove the vignette dimming when disabled. Hurrah.

Just a day later, Alienware released a similar update for this 32 incher. Unfortunately, we just missed the update before our review sample had to be returned. But I'm pretty confident you can consider vignette dimming a solved problem.

And in case you are wondering, while the updated OSD menu does warn you that edge-dimming "is a feature to improve OLED panel durability", Dell has not said that disabling it voids the three-year warranty, which could have been a worry.

So, yeah, I like the Alienware AW3226Q. I like it a lot. Alienware has specced it cleverly to hit a surprisingly appealing price point. It's not a budget option, obviously. But for an RGB-stripe 4K 32-inch OLED, it's got to be a bit of a bargain. The really tough question is whether I'd go for this or one of the OG 32-inch 4K models based on Samsung's first stab at a QD-OLED panel in that format. You can often grab such monitors, such as the MSI MAG 321UP for even less money. That's a very tough call.
