#3675. Report: James Gunn Ousted Amid Messy Power Struggle Despite Superman’s Success

ClayfaceDC StudiosJames GunnPeter SafranSupergirlSuperman

Yesterday, James Gunn and Peter Safran stepped down from their positions as co-presidents at DC Studios. This was after just four years on the job and only three movies in the new superhero cinematic universe they were overseeing. The pair has now been replaced by ex-Marvel producer Jeremy Latcham, whose evangelical history has given some DC fans pause. So what happened? According to a new report by The Hollywood Reporter, trouble had been brewing for the pair as soon as the Skydance merger went through earlier this year.

According to THR‘s sources, on Friday, November 6, Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz informed the pair that, despite previously being told they would be part of the company moving forward, there had been a “change of plans.” The shake-up had reportedly been in the works since “early fall,” with Latcham having been contacted about potentially taking over DC Studios by Skydance Motion Picture Group co-chair John Greenstein, who worked with Latcham during his time at Marvel.

THR says that there were multiple points of “tension” between Gunn and Safran on one hand and the Skydance execs on the other. Gunn and Safran initially reported directly to Warner Bros. CEO David Zaslav, and their contracts said they would maintain that kind of direct reporting structure even in the event of a change in leadership, so they would have reported to Ellison following the merger. Meanwhile, Greenstein and co-chair Dana Goldberg were reportedly trying to consolidate movie production under their leadership, while Gunn and Safran had grown “accustomed to having strong control” over anything under the DC Studios banner.

Other points of contention included that Gunn and Safran were reportedly âslowâ and “not forthcoming” in sharing plans and footage with the Skydance leads.

Many will point to Supergirl‘s box office bomb as a sticking point, and I’ve even seen a lot of people joke that Gunn and Safran only got “one bad movie” before they were thrown out. While Supergirl‘s performance is noted as a problem by THR‘s sources, apparently even their biggest hit, Superman, wasn’t doing enough in the eyes of their corporate overlords. That film, which grossed $618 million on a $225 budget, “did not net out, or have the kind of pop culture impact, in the way that kind of movie should,” in the eyes of Skydance.

Sources say that Gunn is “somewhat relieved” to be out of the business side of things and now focusing on filmmaking. His DC next film, Man of Tomorrow, is set to premiere next year.

As for Latcham, THR‘s sources call him a “down-the-middle shooter” who is more concerned with making “hits for the masses” than Gunn, whose projects often feature somewhat profane writing and obscure characters.

Clayface, the last DC Studios project produced while Gunn and Safran were company co-presidents, is in theaters now.

Capcom still hasn't announced a release date for Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance, the Sunbreak-scale DLC that was revealed in February, but it seems like we might be getting a chance to sample the expansion before too long. A recent Steam listing update has provided a strong reason to suspect that there'll be a public beta for Ascendance available ahead of its launch in 2027.

As SteamDB changelogs show, the Steam app entry for Monster Hunter Wilds' 2024 public beta was quietly updated early this morning to change the app's name from "Monster Hunter Wilds Beta test" to "Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance Beta test." Similarly, the listing's visual assets were updated to feature key art of a hunter facing an Arateka, one of the new monsters being introduced in the expansion.

And sure enough, while the Wilds beta was removed from player libraries after it ended, it's possible for users who'd previously played it to confirm its listing changes within the Steam app by viewing their own played games from their Steam profile. I just looked. It says Ascendance right there.

As the previous Wilds beta consisted of a repackaged demo build, it's likely that an Ascendance beta would follow suit: I'd expect a similar set of hunts to what in-person attendees were able to get hands-on time with at Tokyo Game Show in September, offering a chance to try out the new Boost Bracer weapon mechanics in Master Rank combat.

If a beta does materialize, it'll hopefully be a smoother experience than what beta hunters got in 2024. The early Wilds playtest was the first time PC players encountered the dreaded origami monsters, a symptom of the severe optimization issues that tanked Wilds' reputation for over a year after launch.

As for when that beta might be available, we can only speculate—but given that Monster Hunter has made prior appearances at Geoff Keighley productions, a public playtest that accompanies a hypothetical Game Awards trailer makes intuitive sense. But I'm just reading the tea leaves here—Capcom hasn't said a word about when it'll offer its next DLC teaser.

Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance is set to launch some time in 2027.

Sony has just announced that Grand Theft Auto 6 has become "the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store". Note, it's not the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation history, just on its digital PlayStation Store.

#3672. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

If you pre-ordered a digital version of GTA VI, you can preload it right now, and considering its massive file-size, getting a nine-day head start on that download might be a good idea. But in addition to announcing the pre-load, Rockstar Games has revealed some extra information on the game’s specifications and features, and a brief but glittery new trailer to accompany the announcement.

The biggest thing on the list of specifications is the framerate. Sorry to anyone hoping for a buttery-smooth 60 FPS on console but GTA VI, according to Rockstar, is “targeting 30 frames per second.” That word “targeting” seems especially fraught, suggesting you might not even get all 30 frames all the time.

Rockstar warns that trying to stream the game might lead to some technical difficulties. “Connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay,” Rockstar’s announcement reads. “GTAVI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox.”

"A raucous, absurd spin-off that manages to still feel like a first-rate Yakuza game despite the leftfield setting and delightfully unhinged plot," wrote Matt Elliott in Eurogamer's Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii review.

Meanwhile, Atomfall - Rebellion's quirky British take on a Fallout-like post-apocalyptic idea - was awarded three out of five stars. "If you can get over a difficult start and fancy a lean take on the survival genre, Atomfall delivers an intriguing tale worth discovering," Tom Orry wrote in Eurogamer's Atomfall review. It's presumably been significantly patched and smoothed since then.

The Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake also scored three out of five stars. "Some excellent enhancements make this the ultimate version of Dragon Quest 3, but it could still do more to make it wholly welcoming to newcomers," Daniella Lucas wrote in Eurogamer's Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D review.

We didn't review Hell Let Loose, but the popular World War 2 shooter would go on to amass a serious following and spawn a follow-up game in Hell Let Loose: Vietnam recently, which we did review. "The lavish jungles, rigid command structure, and emphasis on communication make Hell Let Loose: Vietnam a fascinating war simulator when it works. But its many variables can all too easily devolve into a miserable snipe-fest," Rick Lane wrote.

There's plenty to be getting on with, then.

Sony also announced in the PlayStation Blog post it's retiring the PS Plus app on PC from 10th December. Why? Because nobody really uses it.

"With a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4 percent) using the PlayStation Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use," Sony wrote. "As a result, the PlayStation Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available."

While Donald Trump and the White House have engaged in verbal back-and-forths with several late-night talk show hosts, the bulk of those have arguably been with Jimmy Kimmel. The Live! star has notably taken multiple shots at POTUS over the years and received blistering responses as a result. In more than a few of those cases, Kimmel has directly addressed the sentiments shared by Trump and co. on air. And, just recently, Kimmel responded to the assertion that he supposedly has a “peanut-sized brain.”

It’s during Jimmy Kimmel Live!’s opening monologues that viewers typically hear the titular host’s thoughts on President Trump and other political matters. During the November 9 broadcast that aired amid the 2026 TV schedule, Kimmel discussed a statement that was recently released by White House spokesperson Davis Dingle. As can be seen on YouTube, Kimmel laid out the message, which not only included comments about his intelligence but also took aim at his skills as a host and more:

Then the White House got back to the important business of attacking me. I got another statement from White House spokesboy Davis Dingle, who wrote, ‘Jimmy Kimmel’s case of Trump Derangement Syndrome is so advanced that it has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain. He’s far more entertaining when you’re laughing at him than with him. But unfortunately, his real talent is his failing ratings.

Just weeks ago, Dingle chastised Kimmel via another statement and, at that point, he declared that the media personality was “so devoid of actual talent that nobody with any common sense would ever watch him unless it was to laugh at his miserable failures.” And, days prior, President Trump insulted Kimmel as well, calling him a “loser” after the host made jokes about the attendance level at his recent rallies. Kimmel responded with quips while recapping those situations on air, and he did the same thing this time around.

Ultimately, Kimmel didn’t seem too fazed by the sentiments shared by Dingle. With that, he proceeded to share a jokey pitch to the White House employee:

Sick burn, bro. You know what? You should enter a rap battle spitting dope rhymes like that.

Kimmel didn’t finish there, as he also mused that “Trump now has interns insulting me.” As of this writing, the WH hasn’t responded to that “rap battle” comment. Overall, though, this marks just another chapter in the Kimmel/White House/Trump saga. The verbal skirmishes have become so notable at this point that fellow late-night TV hosts Seth Meyers and John Oliver have joked that Trump hates Kimmel the most amongst them and their peers. Kimmel hasn’t just dropped jokes when discussing the current administration, though.

At this point, Kimmel is of the belief that the late-night TV world is “being poisoned” in part due to this political landscape. Months ago, he was also asked what he believed would help save the format, and Kimmel got political by saying, “A different president would be a good start.” On that note, President Trump still has two more years in office, and it remains to be seen what kind of barbs his administration will trade with Kimmel moving forward.

Jimmy Kimmel Live! airs weeknights at 11:35 p.m. ET on ABC.

#3668. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Has A Massive Second-Act Change That Took My Breath Away

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Last night in my playthrough of Ocarina of Time, I finished up the Fire Temple and headed (as one does) to Zora Domain, expecting it to be (as the rest of the game has been so far) very much like the original in structure, just visually more elaborate. And it was, mostly. But as I passed through the realm, I also encountered one of my favorite new additions to the remake so far, one that simultaneously clears up one of Ocarina of Time‘s long-enduring inconsistencies, while also adding pretty significant elements of both horror and hope to the original story.

In the original Ocarina of Time, Zora Domain in the adult timeline is completely frozen over. When Link enters, there are no Zora to be foundâjust an iced-over pond and a frozen waterfall. At the top, you can find King Zora, encased in red ice. Through your adventures in Ice Cavern and later Water Temple, you learn that Ganondorf is (of course) responsible, and that all the Zora have been completely frozen. Sheik was able to save Ruto, who goes on to become the Sage of Water, and you’re later able to thaw out King Zora using Blue Fire.

But the fate of the rest of the Zora is sort of…ambiguous. Presumably due to technical limitations in the original, Zora Domain in adult timeline remains frozen over even post-Water Temple, and the Zora people are nowhere to be found. It’s just King Zora, sitting on his icy throne, for the rest of the game, and Ruto now effectively dead to the world in the Sacred Realm as a sage. You do see some Zora in the credits sequence at the end of the game, implying that some survived, but just what happened to Hyrule’s aquatic folk more broadly remains pretty murky.

The remake clears that up, but the way it does this made me say “holy shit”Â out loud several times.

When you enter Zora Domain as adult Link, you’re treated to a souped-up version of the same sight: frozen pond, frozen waterfall, frozen everything. New to the remake is a haunting new piece of music that does a great job of conveying the frozen emptiness you’re faced with. I hate that you can occasionally hear snippets of the main Zora theme instruments creeping in between the weird, spooky noises! Agh!

But even worse (read: better) than this is what you see when you go out onto the pond. And look down. Into the ice.

Uh, yeah. That’s what that is. That’s where they are. They are actively frozen beneath their own pond. You can just. See them. Down there. Trapped. Dead? Effectively tortured by cold?! Holy shit.

I haven’t finished the Water Temple yet. I considered waiting until I had finished it to write this blog, but I decided to write it now because I wanted to talk about the other emotion, aside from horror, that seeing this inspired. If the Zora are in there now, that opens the door for them to be freed when I finish Water Temple. There are no technical limitations prohibiting Nintendo from thawing out Zora Domain when the time comes and giving these people their lives back. Can Ruto and I really, truly, conclusively save the Zora this time around?

Right now, I am loving the anticipation! I can’t wait to finish the Water Temple tonight, and while I’m a little afraid of being disappointed by the outcome in case Nintendo decided to leave the Zora in this horrible frozen state until the credits, the overall excellence and attention to detail of the Ocarina of Time remake so far has given me ample reason for hope.

#3667. Will Josh O’Connor Be The Next James Bond?

Let’s clear up any potential misunderstandings: there are no official announcements on who will play James Bond at this time. But a British tabloid says that a conversation at a pub has revealed the top-secret casting—if an anonymously sourced rumor is to be believed.

A long list of stars are reportedly auditioning for the 007 role, but even former James Bond Pierce Brosnan says the casting process is a mystery. “I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire.”

According to UK publication The Sun, the decision is rumored to have been made: a recent colleague of Josh O’Connor, a 36-year-old actor from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, says Disclosure Day star has been cast in the role. If true, Turner beat out likely contenders including Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

Josh O'Connor at UK premiere for Disclosure Day on June 04, 2026.

The news comes as a bit of a game of telephone. Until last week, O'Connor was in the case of Golden Boy, Clifford Odets' 1937 drama about a violin player turned boxer in Depression-era New York City. Citing the claims of one of O'Connor's cast mates, an unnamed source tells The Sun “I bumped into one of Josh’s Golden Boy cast mates at The French House."

“Out of nowhere, and oiled by a few glasses of lager, they blurted out that Josh was the next James Bond."

When the source pushed back, the thespian grew more insistent. “They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween," a claim that implies the decision has been made for over a week.

Josh O'Connor, winner of the Outstanding Lead Actor In A Drama Series award for The Crown, at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards on September 19, 2021.

If this rumor comes to fruition, it would not be the first time O'Connor took on an iconic UK role. In 2021, he took home the outstanding lead actor Emmy for his role as then-Prince, now-King Charles III, in Netflix series The Crown. While in his role as the future king, he was encouraged to tap into a side that one might not expect.

“It’s Prince Charles as Walter White," he told The Guardian in 2020, making a reference to crime series Breaking Bad. "Our job was to make people feel sorry for [Charles], so that in season four, when he turns into this at times monstrous character, we understand how he got there.” A heel turn that isn't unBond, especially the darker Bond we grew used to with Daniel Craig. (Craig, in fact, has a direct connection to O’Connor, as the pair co-starred in Knives Out: Wake Up Dead Man.)

Speaking with the BBC, O'Connor did not confirm the casting rumor—but he didn't deny it either. (Vanity Fair has reached out to O'Connor's representatives for comment, but has not yet received a response.)

"To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary," O'Connor said this week.

"It's an incredibly bizarre pinch me moment...even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that. But I am afraid, there is nothing to say beyond that."

Fairgames was revealed in 2023, but nothing more was ever seen of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Bloomberg report says Fairgames, a PvP heist shooter announced by Haven Studios and Sony in 2023, has been cancelled. In something of a surprising twist, a PlayStation rep told the site there will be no layoffs as a result of the cancellation, as Haven will "shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities."

While it was announced three years ago, work on Fairgames appears to have started even further back, in 2021. Just a couple months after her high-profile split with Google Stadia, Assassin's Creed co-creator Jade Raymond announced the formation of Haven Studios, which was "working on an unannounced new IP for PlayStation."

In 2022, right around the time former PlayStation boss Jim Ryan was talking about launching 12 live service games by 2025, Sony acquired the studio outright; a year after that, Fairplay was revealed to the world.

But things have not gone smoothly since then. Helldivers 2 was a massive hit, but seven of those planned games were cancelled before release. Of the remaining games, one was Marathon, which endures but has not lived up to expectations, and another was Concord, one of the most famously disastrous game launches in years, which was taken offline less than two weeks after it launched, never to return. A live-service spinoff of the Horizon series, Hunters Gathering, was also reportedly rebooted after negative feedback from playtests.

A partial accounting of canned multiplayer projects:

The Concord catastrophe in particular seemed to shake Sony, which began reversing its live service strategy just a few months later. Fairgames itself looked to be in trouble in 2025 when Raymond departed Haven, reportedly after an external playtest left PlayStation leadership "concerned about how the game was received and its progress."

The Bloomberg report says a more recent large-scale playtest produced similar results. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set,” PlayStation executives Sean Decker and John Doyle wrote in an email sent to Haven Studios employees. "Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

The one bright spot to the cancellation is that no jobs will be cut because of it: A Sony rep told Bloomberg that Haven "will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities."

It appears the Barefoot Contessa knew a thing or two about Batman's travel plans.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I spend a lot of time keeping up with the 2026 movie schedule and all the upcoming superhero movies, but Jennifer Garner left me thinking about a Batman production from a decade ago. The actress recently shared a fond memory involving Ben Affleck, Ina Garten and an unforgettable family trip to Paris. I love that the Caped Crusader barely scratches the surface of what made it so special.

During a conversation on Happy Hour with Ina Garten, the 13 Going on 30 actress recalled taking her children overseas while Affleck was filming in London. Apparently, the comic book movie production provided the perfect excuse to get out of town for a while. Garner explained:

When my kids were little, I went to Paris. Ben was shooting some Batman-ish movie in London, and we went for six weeks. I took them out of school. It was the last time I really took kids out of school, but it was wonderful. It was incredible. It was so fun.

I recently revisited Affleck and Garner's time making Daredevil together, so hearing her describe his later superhero blockbuster as some "Batman-ish movie" is especially funny. I imagine Affleck had a few more specific words for the project, but I appreciate Garner remembers the family adventure rather than whatever Bruce Wayne was getting up to at the time.

Her timing also helps identify the film. While Justice League arrived in theaters in 2017, Affleck and the production spent months filming in London the previous year. Reports from that April confirmed that Garner and their three children planned to stay in the U.K. during production. By May, the family had also been spotted vacationing in Paris. So, despite the wonderfully vague description, Justice League appears to be our Batman-ish culprit.

There's a bittersweet wrinkle to the timeline. Garner and Affleck announced their separation in 2015, before the trip, and officially filed for divorce in 2017. Their divorce was finalized the following year. That makes this a particularly sweet memory of their family life during a complicated period. The two have maintained a close co-parenting relationship since, with Garner recently praising Affleck for helping care for their children while she works.

Apparently, we have Ina Garten to thank for one of Garner's favorite memories from the trip. With her youngest son, Samuel, only 4 at the time, Garner shared photos of the kids with Garten, who suggested they take a boat ride along the Seine. Really, who am I to argue with the Barefoot Contessa about how to spend an afternoon in Paris?

Garner recalled cruising down the river as the city began lighting up around them, and the experience stuck with her. She's since made a point of doing it whenever she returns to Paris, and looking back at those original photos still reminds her of how happy the kids were. She told Garten that her suggestion made the whole thing "such an adventure." I love that something as simple as taking a boat ride became one of those family memories she keeps coming back to.

Garten's Paris recommendations didn't stop there. Years later, when Garner returned with her eldest daughter Violet, she texted her friend for another round of suggestions. This time Garten sent them to a handbag boutique, a cheese shop, a specialty food market and a restaurant specializing in soufflés. Violet apparently enjoyed the itinerary so much that she retraced their steps while studying abroad. Now I'm wondering how I get Ina Garten's number before my next vacation.

I like hearing Garner speak so fondly about those days, especially knowing what was happening in her personal life at the time. It also makes me wonder how many wonderful family memories get made while Hollywood's biggest productions happen in the background.

Affleck might have been busy bringing his take on The Dark Knight to life; his wife and kids were apparently having an adventure all their own. Something tells me those Paris photographs mean a whole lot more to her than another superhero movie ever could.

#3662. Mortal Kombat 2 Is Winning The Race To Become Mortal Kombat 2

What's in a name? That's the question that Mortal Kombat studio CCO Ed Boon is asking, as he recently set up a few polls asking for opinions on what the next Mortal Kombat game should be called. According to Boon, three possible names were on the table: Mortal Kombat 12, Mortal Kombat 13, or Mortal Kombat 2.

"Footnote: Some people are assuming the title with the most votes will determine where we take the story," Boon wrote online. "That’s not the case. We’ve just had difficulty kounting lately."

The current naming convention for Mortal Kombat doesn't make much sense if you've taken a break from the franchise. The series made a successful comeback in 2011 with Mortal Kombat, the ninth installment in the franchise. This was followed by Mortal Kombat X in 2015 and Mortal Kombat 11 in 2019, which brought the original storyline that began in 1992's Mortal Kombat to a close. This was followed by a soft reboot in 2023 with Mortal Kombat 1, which remixed established story beats and put familiar characters in new roles.

To make things even more confusing, Mortal Kombat 1 heavily references multiple timelines toward the end of its campaign, drawing in characters from across a Mortal Kombat multiverse for a final showdown against Shang Tsung from the previous timeline. The Khaos Reigns expansion would also touch on these ideas, as the Titan version of Havik sought to merge all timelines into one.

Currently, "Mortal Kombat 2" is leading the votes with 45.2% of people polled by Boon favoring that title, at the time of writing. If this becomes the title of the next Mortal Kombat game, it will be the second Mortal Kombat 2, which will probably confuse anyone who hasn't been following along. While it hasn't been officially revealed yet, Boon did confirm that Mortal Kombat developer NetherRealm Studios is "pursuing another Mortal Kombat game," and he added that "other forms of media and whatnot" for the Mortal Kombat franchise are in development.

That was back in May, and since then, Mortal Kombat's parent company, Warner Bros. Interactive, has seen some big changes. Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery eventually went through, leading to the merger between Warner Bros. Interactive and Paramount Games Studio. That new entity puts Mortal Kombat, Game of Thrones, Batman, and a treasure trove of IP under the same roof as Avatar: The Last Airbender, South Park, and Star Trek. Tony Driscoll, president of games and experiences at Skydance, will oversee the new division.

#3661. Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles, and Queen Camilla Gather For Remembrance Day

This Sunday, November 8, King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Kate Middleton, Prince William, Princess Anne and other members of the royal family came together to observe Remembrance Sunday, one of the most solemn events on the United Kingdom's calendar. The day marks the anniversary of the armistice that ended World War I, signed on “the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month” in 1918.

The focal point of every Remembrance Day is the Cenotaph in Whitehall, the Portland stone monument where tribute is paid to those who fell in the wars and conflicts in which the country has participated. Every year, representatives of the royal family, political leaders, the Armed Forces, and veterans gather there: This year, more than 10,000 marched alongside the king and the prime minister.

True to tradition, Charles III laid a wreath at the memorial on behalf of the nation and led the royal family. At his side was Prince William, Princess Anne, and the Duke of Edinburgh, who also paid their respects with a floral tribute. Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales, Kate Middleton, watched the ceremony from the balcony of the Foreign Office, as is customary. On the political front, Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath on his first Remembrance Sunday as head of the government, accompanied by Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch and other political leaders.

The day before had already been a day of remembrance: the King, the Queen, and the Princes of Wales attended the Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall, the major tribute to the armed forces that precedes Remembrance Sunday.

#3660. A Big Talk About Big Walk’s AI Fallout

Big Walk, the game that was likely at or near the top of a lot of people’s game of the year lists, was made in very small part with the use of AI. This was not previously disclosed publicly or on Steam because, according to House House’s statement on the matter, “the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” And we’re only finding out about this now, long after the game has released to universal acclaim, because Big Walk was apparently at the heart of a fractious discussion about AI usage in development and the game’s eligibility for awards among the jury members for the 2027 Independent Games Festival.

Over the past month, IGF judges and jurists have had intense, difficulty, generous, and deeply engaged conversations about AI and the games industry.

This statement is the result of those conversations.

— austin_walker (@austinwalker.bsky.social) 2026-11-09T22:42:15.552Z

Some jurors felt that a hard, no-exceptions line needed to be drawn in the sand, and made a public, signed statement to that effect. Others felt that considering how House House used the tech was worth consideration in determining Big Walk‘s eligibility. House House claims that “well under 0.1% of Big Walkâs code had anything to do with this usage and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game,” and it seems like some jurors felt that such limited use shouldn’t disqualify a game that was very likely in the running for the Seumas McNally Grand Prize, the IGF’s top award.

The discussions about this event at Kotaku mirror those playing out amongst gamers and developers on social media. But at the heart of it all, this sucks man.

Ash Parrish: Where do you all come down on this? Rebekah Valentine: As the person on this team who went to bat, hard, for this game, who loved it completely, who bullied you all so much to play it and wrote about it incessantly, I will start by saying: God damn it.

Ash: I have not played the game because I havenât taken the time to round up friends to play it with. It was important that I make an effort to try because this game seems so special to everyone Iâve seen talk about it. This whole thing, not just how AI was used but how we found out about it, definitely removes that urgency. Rebekah: I am not naive enough to believe that every game I play has zero AI touching it in any way. In fact, I assume many of them do. But I, and I think many others, made an assumption that based on the past stances of this dev team and their general attention to a lot of hand-crafted detail, AI would not even be a factor.Â

Carolyn Petit: I’m actually playing it right now with friends and it was certainly strange to emerge from our play session last night (for those whoâve played it, we just got the ski lift working!) and into the online discourse. My feeling is that the goal should be an expectation of zero AI usage on any level. It’s stolen labor no matter how you cut it. Does that mean I think House House should be crucified in the court of public opinion? Maybe not, but I do think we need to be clear about establishing and holding to that expectation moving forward, and I donât think it should receive honors at IGF. John Walker: I think itâs really important to recognize that of all the games weâve loved this year, almost all of them will have used LLMs as part of the coding process. I hate that, and I wish they had not, and I appeal to developers to stop doing it. But of all of the games to do this, I suspect Big Walk did it about the very least. So I feel like this is a public flogging that will achieve demoralizing or demolishing a great studio and little else. Ash: Then why not tell us up front and give consumers the choice? I think a lot of people would have been OK with the exact disclosure we were given today. That folks did not have that option to choose feels way worse than the fact AI was used at all. John: I believe the reason why (and again, this isnât my justifying it, but trying to sum up why it happens) is becauseâ¦itâs what everyone does. You run the code through the tool to check for errors. Or you ask the tool to suggest a way to code to fix the issue. And because thatâs the expected action of someone using the coding tools, itâs incredibly easy to forget this is the same world-destroying mechanism that powers the plagiarism art and military drones. Carolyn: Right, but the fact that it’s what everyone does doesn’t mean we should be okay with it. If anything, it’s precisely why we need to be so clear about saying no.

Ash: And weâve got people posting on social media that theyâve seemingly solved the exact problem House House ran into, without using AI.

John: I donât know how much more clearly I can say that I donât think we should be OK with it. Iâm trying to answer the question, âWhy was it used at all?â Carolyn: But you seem to be taking an issue with people taking an issue with it. John: No, Iâm taking an issue with people trying to win an internet battle of virtue by trying to out-hate everyone else, and suggesting that thereâs a better way to convince the vast majority of developers to not do this.

Carolyn: I don’t think we do that without deploying shame to some degree.

John: I find publicly shaming one of the least offending offenders in order to teach the world a lesson a really horrid way to go about discourse. Ash: But wouldnât you agree that having such a public discussion about how this whole thing has gone down is at least an attempt to signal, âHey devs, you donât want this to happen, so donât do thisâ? Like this discussion is the way we try to signal this is not a thing we want and that devs should try to find another way around their problems. And maybe itâs an imperfect way, but itâs something.

Carolyn: Yes. I also think the statement from some jury members was great. And I don’t think we can ignore that this one hurts more than some disposable top-to-bottom AI slop on Steam because of how well-received Big Walk is and because of the dev teamâs commendable stance on things like BDS.

Rebekah: Itâs a really complicated thing to think and talk about and I have a lot of conflicting thoughts here.

On one hand, I share Carolynâs opinion that I want zero AI usage on any level. And I want the industry to take steps toward that. I think the IGF judgesâ statement is a great move to that end, and I support it. More groups, more award shows, should make such statements and stick to such convictions.

I also think I see a bit of what John is saying here and why heâs saying it. I think that House House has generally demonstrated itself to be a group of thoughtful developers (see: the BDS boycott), and their statement now reflects this. This, as Carolyn says, makes what feels like a betrayal more hurtful. But I also do believe them based on past actions when they say they feel not having a policy about this is a failure and that they are going to address that. A lot of the public response Iâve seen to this has been to deem the whole game as slop, to condemn them utterly, and treating this as an irredeemable offense. It sounds like some of the behind-the-scenes discussion on IGF was like that too. And I donât really agree with that. Iâd rather this open a discussion publicly about why they felt this was necessary and help both House House and other devs in their position come around to better ways of doing things. What Iâm afraid will happen instead (and what some seem to be doing already) is that theyâll just get deemed a slop studio and thatâs that. Meanwhile, hundreds of other, bigger studios with far worse morals will skate on by without ever disclosing anything.

Again, to be clear, I donât think we solve that problem by not talking about it and by not shaming it. I reiterate that I am really upset and betrayed by this, a problem that was so easy to avoid! I just wish there were a better way to have industry-wide conversations generally. Bluesky, Twitter, and social media in general donât seem to be it. John: I too want zero AI use! Rebekah: I also want to recognize that Iâm feeling both betrayed by them and maybe a little defensive of them because I loved the game so much. And also that my own view of discussions on social media is incomplete and not reflective of the broader consensus. Iâm not a dev. This stuff is hard, man. Itâs easy to say Iâm anti-AI. The more I try to put it into practice though, the harder it is to do, because this crap keeps popping up everywhere, unexpectedly, unasked for, unwanted.

Ash: And thatâs only the stuff we know about. And I think my genuine disaffection comes from the lack of disclosure.

John: I wonder if any of us manages not to have AI be in at least 0.1 percent of our lives. Every time I search something in the Chrome taskbar and forget itâll be a Gemini screed of gibberish, but with a useful link. Or when I click on the âchat nowâ button on the medical site I use, and have to fight past the AI to get to a person. Ash: I mean thatâs a structural issue, isnât it? Some of us would, if the structures undergirding our lives would allow us, choose to be totally AI-free. We should have at least nominally more power over that in our leisure time, no? Or we could attempt to exert more power over that if developers allow us to make that choice.

Rebekah: Like as a journalist, if Iâm struggling to answer a question, there are a lot of things Iâll do to get an answer. Ask people. Research primary sources online. Read newspapers. Send emails, make calls, talk to experts, look into communities. Asking Claude or ChatGPT or whatever doesnât even occur. Like, it never once enters onto my list of, âthis is a potential way to find a solution.â So I have questions about why it was even a consideration for them at all.

But also, so many people in my life use ChatGPT without even thinking about it. Like, itâs a non-issue to them, not remotely controversial. I donât know these devs personally, I donât know what they know about the harms it perpetuates. I feel like they should know based on their previously stated politics, but, people are inscrutable!

I guess at minimum we can say they know now. I will expect a disclosure on their next game confirming no AI was used. If I do not see that disclosure I will not buy it. Not because I adamantly refuse to play any game with even a drop of it in there ever, but because given their past actions I cannot trust that a game with no such disclosure did not use it in ways I do not anticipate or am not comfortable with.

John: Again, Iâm just thinking about being a developer using the tools developers have access to. They are all riddled with AI. Try avoiding that shit in Photoshop.

Ash: And Iâm saying if, because of the structures theyâre forced into, devs are required to use AI in the process of their development, I can understand and possibly forgive its use. But you gotta tell me so I can make that choice myself.

John: Itâs even harder, because Steam directly tells them not to declare its use in coding.

Rebekah: That is another thing thatâs worth mentioning though. Unityâs stuffed with AI crap. And Unity, critically, was apparently very unhelpful to them when they asked for assistance solving their coding problems. Unity I think deserves a big olâ pile of heat for its role in this as well.

Carolyn: This is why I think that if we donât set a very clear expectation of no AI use, it will just continue to seep into everything even more and more. So yes, that means putting pressure on Unity to not build it into their tools, and if they continue to do so, it means pressuring devs not to use Unity. And so on. Obviously the people with all the money at the top of these institutions want it employed so they can save money on labor. We have to tell them thatâs not gonna fly.

John: Someone said to me today that going after the developers is like going after smokers, and that we should instead be going after the companies that release the poison. I see their point, but also think you have to explain to smokers why smoking is so incredibly dangerous to them and those around them. But to take their point, it would be far more effective to shame Valve into including coding AI declarations than to pressure each individual developer into publicly shaming themselves.

Ash: I understand AIâs ubiquity makes that hard, but if we want to get rid of this shit or at least discourage its use, we gotta draw the line somewhere. But I agree that Unity, Valve, etc needs to come up more in this discussion.

Rebekah: This is not to remotely take the blame off House House, but for this to work we need to find ways to get more AAA studios on board, and I donât know how we do that. Not to say we should throw our hands in the air and give up, I just donât know where to begin pressuring major companies. Boycotts famously are not meaningfully impactful at the AAA level. I would really like to see people organize around finding solutions to that. Ash: I think it means getting a developer like House House to say âBecause of this, weâre gonna use Godot going forward.â Which I understand is incredibly easy for a non-developer to say. But we gotta coalition-build here. And having these arguments might be a baby step toward something like that.

I want to encourage folks to participate in these conversations at the community level and find ways to organize around it and affect change within their groups, whether thatâs devs, consumers, media, whatever. Arguing on social media about it is cathartic but ultimately not super helpful. Ash: I think they know pretty well at this point. Rebekah: Sure, but again I think thereâs a difference between a lot of people yelling on social media and emailing them for comment, and someone who loved their game emailing them to tell them how this personally affects them

Ash: Coalition building! Seems maybe silly to ask, but is this game still your GOTY Rebekah? Carolyn? John? John: Iâm afraid, as a misanthrope, Iâve not played it. Carolyn: Iâm just playing it now. It was definitely shaping up to be on my list (probably not at the top but on the list somewhere), but now Iâll have to give it some thought. Rebekah: I honestly donât know what to do about it. While we’ve been patiently awaiting news on Shang-Chi 2, Marvel is bringing back Simu Liu for the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday. So, like many other MCU stars awaiting Secret Wars filming, the man has been trying to stay fit. He recently took a note from Inde Navarette when it comes to Marvel workouts, and trolled Saturday Night Live’s recent Shane Gillis gaffe in the same video.

I’m sure Marvel was super happy about getting roped in to the Shane Gillis monologue controversy, which involved the Tires star joking about women wearing little clothing at the gym these days. (He also capped these comments by calling them “whores,” which is probably what made the story go as viral as it did.) Anyway, Shane Gillis made the joke at Studio 8H, and then a week later Inde Navarette referenced it while talking about working out to play one of the X-Men in her own SNL monologue.

This is where Simu Liu comes in. The man came out of the wood work this week to cheekily show off a gym workout. He superimposed the video with Inde Navarette’s SNL monologue comments, and captioned the video, “time to put on my little outfit…”

Listen, this isn’t the first time Simu Liu has had a little fun trolling on the Internet, and I feel confident in guessing it won’t be the last. Just a couple of months ago he had a little fun with the MCU movies in order, and asked fans to “please help [him] support this little indie feature,” above a poster for Avengers: Doomsday, which will likely make over a billion dollars. Then, there was that time he joked about the Spider-Man leaks when Andrew Garfield and Tobey Maguire were involved in one of Tom Holland's popular films.

He can take it as well as dish it out, though. Early in his career, he modeled for some stock photos, and the Internet LOVES to bring it up. But he's taken the comments on the chin.

Right now, Marvel is in between films, so if you’re going to troll about the MCU, now’s a good time for a star to get a little attention for it. While schlepping relatively low weights is not as impressive as, say, one-armed pull-ups, it’s a good way to keep the fanbase engaged as Doomsday gets closer.

Avengers: Doomsday hits the 2026 release schedule around the holidays, and is in theaters opposite Dune 3, which has earned it the moniker Dunesday. Meanwhile, Chris Hemsworth has remained swole, and it has people wondering if he’s getting ready for Secret Wars. On the other hand, Simu Liu has already confirmed he's in both.

#3658. GTA 6 Preloading Is Officially Live, Files Mention Multiplayer And PS5 Pro Features

At long last, you can now install Grand Theft Auto 6 on your console via preloading, or at least you can if you live in Australia or New Zealand. Preloading begins in all regions at midnight local time, so people in the US are almost there.

With preloading now live, people have dug through the files and found things they weren't intended to see. That includes references to things like "join Session," "launch Activity," and "launch Multiplayer Activity." People are taking these to be references to a new form of GTA Online.

Rockstar has said GTA 6 is a single-player game, but it’s expected to add some form of online multiplayer at some point. Just because "Multiplayer" was found in the game's files, that doesn't necessarily mean online functionality will be available at launch--it's likely coming sometime later.

People have theorized that GTA 6's story and Online could be separate games. That remains to be seen, but those who have the game preloaded have discovered that GTA 6's "Story" is an individual download within the game's files. Whatever the case, experts and insiders believe GTA 6's new online experience will launch at some point in 2027.

Additionally, the datamining effort led to some discoveries about what Rockstar might be cooking up in terms of PS5 Pro support. People believe they found references to 120Hz support on PS5 Pro, along with multi-frame super resolution, which is known as PSSR on PS5 Pro.

Rockstar has yet to announce any specifics about GTA 6 for PS5 Pro, and the game's trailers so far have been captured on a standard PS5.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. For more, check out the exact worldwide launch times. #3657. Former PlayStation Boss Thinks Sony Is Solving The Wrong Problem With PS6

Sony confirmed last week that development on its "next-generation" PlayStation platform will pick up speed in 2027, but not everyone is convinced the world needs a PS6 right now. In an interview with The Trophy Room, former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden said true innovation would come from finding a way to lower the price of the PS5, allowing more potential buyers to enter the market.

"I think we have enough power in the machine. The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1,200, it's to make another PS5 for $300. Now, that would be true innovation," Layden said, while also remarking how the PS5 generation saw price increases over time, not reductions.

Compared to previous generations, the PS5 has only gotten more expensive in the six years that it has been on the market, rising from $400 to $600 for the PS5 Digital Edition, while the PS5 with a disc drive has increased from $500 to $650. The PS5 Pro has seen the biggest increase in the few years it has been around, as the beefier machine has jumped from its original price of $700 to $900. Various factors are to blame, but one of the biggest is the global memory shortage that has hit all fields of technology, thanks to AI data centers eating into the world's supply.

A PS6 that costs over $1,000 will be out of reach for many consumers, and as Layden believes, it likely won't be as big a graphical leap forward as we've seen in previous PlayStation generations. While the difference in video game graphics between the PS1 and the PS2 was especially noticeable, later consoles have shown diminishing returns, and Layden believes the graphical quality of PS6 games will be even harder to notice. "These are the differences that only dogs can hear," Layden said about the reported increase in teraflops and ray-tracing power the PS6 will supposedly offer.

"What the company needs to do is do what it's never done, which is don't iterate the console. Make it smaller, make it cheaper, do all the things you can around that. The silicon is fine, the operating system is fine. It's more than enough power to build the kind of games all of us want to play."

As the current generation continues, Sony has also sought to extend the PS5's lifespan with new ideas, like a PS5 Pro-inspired upscaling tech called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR). While it's only available for two games currently, QSSR could give the PS5 plenty of staying power in the current gaming generation and the next.

#3656. LACMA Art+Film Gala: Nicole Kidman, Timothée Chalamet Honor Denis Villeneuve

“It’s a pleasure to be here. You guys are just crazy party people,” said artist Vija Celmins as she summed up the jovial atmosphere at the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala during her casual and off-the-cuff acceptance speech as one of the two honorees that night.

The annual fundraiser is a party, and unique among the many galas that hit the town this time of year. Along with raising money for the museum’s initiative to make film more central to its programming (this year it raised a record-breaking almost $7 million), it brings out an eclectic mix of A-list talent, up-and-coming filmmakers, and giants of the art world.

Honoree, Denis Villeneuve, Honoree Vija Celmins, co-chair Eva Chow and LACMA CEO Michael Govan

Just a quick scan of the packed room: Al Pacino sitting with artist Ed Ruscha and art dealer Larry Gagosian; artist Alex Israel wrapping his arm around Orlando Bloom for a photo; model Alex Consani crouching down to chat with influencer and comedian Quenlin Blackwell; and artists Jonas Wood and Mickalene Thomas chatting in one corner while Sarah Paulson and Parker Posey catch up in another.

Anya Taylor-Joy set the mood for the evening as one of the first arrivals on the red carpet, where talent posed in front of Chris Burden’s famed public art installation Urban Light. There in support of Dune director Denis Villeneuve, who was honored along with Celmins, the Dune: Part Two star wore a vintage 1997 Pierre Cardin haute couture bridal gown with a sheer silver overlay that looked both of the past and of the future.

Villeneuve’s leading man, Timothée Chalamet, skipped the carpet altogether, instead slipping into the crowded tent for dinner in a seat next to Villeneuve and his wife, producer Tanya Lapointe. Chalamet arrived separately from girlfriend Kylie Jenner, who did walk the carpet in a low-back Ashi Studio gown. When Jenner arrived at her table, she was seated opposite Chalamet, reaching across to grab his hand.

Seated next to Villeneuve was Nicole Kidman (in a voluminous, ballerina-inspired Chanel dress), who flew 15 hours from Australia to give Villeneuve his award. “The truth is I’ve never really met Denis. I’ve met him on some red carpets and sort of waved at him,” she said during her remarks. “Yet somehow I feel like I know the deepest parts of him because that is what extraordinary filmmakers do. They let you in. They reveal themselves to us through their work. They invite you into their imaginations, into their dreams, into their questions, and into their fears.”

Monica Barbaro, Salma Hayek and Kim Kardashian

Before Villeneuve took the stage, a video capturing his film legacy of big, bold, and personal epics like Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, Arrival, and the Dune trilogy was played, featuring a slew of A-list directors singing his praises, including Steven Spielberg, Alfonso Cuarón, Alejandro González Iñárritu, James Cameron, and Chloé Zhao. “I’ve always felt that cinema is seen as a Pop art—the film carries the burden of being popular in the present,” said Villeneuve in his acceptance speech. “But at the end of the day, the real challenge is to make something that can enter the test of time.”

Speaking of tests (screen tests, that is) Villeneuve got a bit playful with the end of his speech, announcing to the room that he would—right here, right now—announce which actor would play James Bond. The French Canadian director is helming the next Bond film, and over the past week reports have been flying about who might be cast. Would Villeneuve put us all out of our misery and spill the beans? “The actor who will play the next James Bond is—and I will stop right now because [producer] Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” he said with a smile.

The gala, once again presented by Gucci, hosted a slew of this Oscar season’s most exciting young filmmakers, including Obsession filmmaker Curry Barker and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman, along with La Bola Negra directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as Los Javis). The latter told me they didn’t plan to party as hard as they did at the Academy Museum Gala a few weeks ago, where they went viral for singing along to Taylor Swift’s performance of “Love Story.” Said Ambrossi, “I’m drinking only water tonight.”

Among the other guests at the gala (which had additional support by Audi), Joel Edgerton chatted with Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson and Daniel Scheinert, one half of the Oscar-winning directing team Daniels (Everything Everywhere All at Once). Kim Kardashian wove her way through the crowd, pausing perfectly to look over her shoulder for a trailing photographer. And several stars made a date night out of the event: Sienna Miller brought fiancé Oli Green; Julia Garner sat with musician Charlie Walker; Viola Davis enjoyed the night with husband and producing partner Julius Tennon. Paris Hilton, who introduced Rosé onstage with her classic catchphrase “that’s hot,” wore a glittering Jenny Packham gown as she cascaded through the room with her husband, Carter Reum.

Eva Chow, who had co-chaired the gala for the past 15 years with Leonardo DiCaprio, announced that she’d be stepping down from her post after this year. Dubbed the “Culture Queen of Los Angeles,” she is credited with bringing together Hollywood and the art world for the event, helping grow it into the must-attend party of the season. DiCaprio couldn’t make it this year because he has a cold, but his girlfriend, model Vittoria Ceretti, was there to represent him.

But with all these big Hollywood types in the room, it was Celmins who stole the show—though she didn’t mean to. In a video that ran before her acceptance speech, the artist welcomed the video crew into her home, revealing her quick-witted humor, her ornery cat (she claims to be a dog person), and her love of Bob Dylan. Celmins is best known for her boundless work inspired by nature, including ocean waves, desert floors, and starry night skies. She charmed the crowd with her boundless personality as well.

LACMA had plenty to celebrate this year too. After a 20-year-long planning and development process, the David Geffen Galleries were completed this past year. As partygoers entered the tent for dinner, the silhouette of the formidable new building stood out in the background. “Same tent. Different buildings around it,” joked LACMA CEO Michael Govan during his opening remarks.

After his speech, Villeneuve and all the guests made their way out to LACMA’s main courtyard, where Rosé would perform under the stars. I joked with him that I thought he would make some news with that tease of a Bond casting, and then wondered if he likes being the center of attention at a gala like this. He said he values the connections he makes with other filmmakers and artists at these events. “I like talking one-on-one,” he said.

Noor Alfallah, Al Pacino, Erica Pelosini, Larry Gagosian and Ed Ruscha

While Rosé performed four songs for the black-tie-clad audience, Emily in Paris star Ashley Park and In the Heights actor Anthony Ramos swayed to her ballad “Number One Girl.” Popcorn and cotton candy were passed out to the audience, which, naturally, sang along when Rosé ended her set with her biggest hit, “APT.” Andrew Garfield led his Artificial costar Monica Barbaro by the hand through the crowd. Though the pair didn’t pose for photos on the carpet together, the couple (who have been romantically linked since 2025) spent the evening in close contact as they chatted with friends like Salma Hayek Pinault.

Villeneuve’s speech best captured the evening’s one-of-a-kind mash-up of art and film when he spoke passionately about the importance of human effort in the era of AI. “I can create something with a prompt, or I can go into the desert with actors, with a crew, and go on a real adventure where I learn about life and become better at my craft,” he said. “More important than the result is the process. The process is how the human experience acquires its meaning. In this moment in time, it is more important than ever that human beings keep making art together.”

Odessa A'zion in a Charles & Ron + Maison Privee coat.

I spend way too much time on wikis reading about spin-off games made for handheld and mobile devices I will probably never play (there was a whole trilogy of Silent Hill: Orphan games that have lived up to their name by being orphaned on old phones). The Elder Scrolls Travels are a prime example—games made in the gap between Morrowind and Oblivion. The third in the series, Shadowkey, came out on Nokia's N-Gage handheld—a cross between a GameBoy Advance and a mobile phone that lasted two years before being discontinued in 2005.

This first-person RPG is about to return thanks to Dan Whelan, whose Shadowkey Reforged project will let us play Shadowkey in widescreen with controller support and upscaled graphics. You can choose to play in classic or modern mode, but you can also toggle individual features one by one. Modern mode isn't just a graphical upgrade as it also adds features from the later mainline Elder Scrolls games like stamina-based sprinting, stealth, and ragdoll physics.

This is one of those times where I prefer the original game's look, as the brutally abrupt draw distance leaves a lot to your imagination while the modernized version seems to show enemies looming unresponsively in the near distance. And it's not like the upscaled character models actually look good, despite being beyond what Nokia's taco phone was capable of displaying.

While Shadowkey was never particularly well-ranked in the pantheon of Elder Scrolls games, people did praise its use of the Morrowind soundtrack, which Shadowkey Reforged will continue. Point it to your Morrowind install and it'll borrow both music and sound effects from the best Elder Scrolls game.

To answer the obvious question, Whelan says in the FAQ: "I used AI to assist with coding and building the engine, and with debugging. I used AI image generation combined with Photoshop and some manual sprite editing to create most of the modern, higher resolution artwork."

Whelan plans to release Shadowkey Reforged on November 11, which is just 18 hours away at the time of writing. You'll be able to download Windows, Mac, and Android versions from the website, though you'll need the original game's files from your Nokia N-Gage as well, or whatever abandonware site you frequent.

#3653. How To Get A Sleeping Bag In World Of Warcraft: Forever

World of WarcraftWorld of Warcraft: Forever

If you’ve been partying up with others in World of Warcraft: Forever, you’ve probably seen a weird sleeping bag item being used by your teammates. You may have even been encouraged to use it yourself, and gotten a little EXP boost for your trouble. Now, having snuggled up in the sleeping bag with four of your dungeoning buddies, maybe you want this nap device for yourself and your own leveling journey. I am here to tell you how to get it. The journey is not without pain and sacrifice.

The Cozy Sleeping Bag is an item first introduced in WoW‘s Season of Discovery. It has unlimited uses on a one-hour-long cooldown. When you use it (the cast takes 15 whole seconds), you place a sleeping bag on the ground. If you stand still on top of it, your character will lay down after a few seconds and take a nap. In this state, you’ll gain a stack of a buff once every minute up to three stacks, with each stack giving you a 1-percent bonus to EXP earned that lasts through death, for two hours. So in total, you spend a little over three minutes to receive a 3-percent bump to EXP gained for two hours. The best part is that you can share this with your party members, so one sleeping bag will give your whole group a buff if everyone takes a nap together.

That said, given how long it takes to obtain, it’s…kind of a worthless reward. You’ll spend about the same amount of time you save in leveling just running all over the place to obtain the bag in the first place. It’s not a toy, so it takes up a precious inventory slot, too. That said, you do also get a 12-slot bag from the questline, which feels truly luxurious early in the game. And you can use this as an opportunity to pick up a bunch of useful flight points you’ll be happy to have later. As Horde, I grabbed flight points at places like Grom’gol, Booty Bay, Tarren Mill, Sunrock Retreat, and Hammerfall. I also did the early steps of this quest simultaneously with getting the Night Watchman’s Torch, which helped “save time” (if you can call any bit of this time-saving).

You’ll need to be at least level 14 to start this quest. Be warned, you will end up running into high-level areas to finish this, and will probably die a lot in the process. My general tip for this is to stay on the main roads whenever you can, as monsters tend to avoid them. However, some areas (like Stranglethorn Vale) will have monsters that will aggro you from off the path, and other places you’ll run through are PvP zones, so you may have to improvise. Just don’t be deceived into thinking that cross-country hikes are the best idea.

The first two steps are the only ones that are different depending on whether you’re Alliance or Horde. Both factions will have to complete both steps, just in reverse order from one another.

Alliance will start in Westfall. For Horde, this is your step two, so be prepared to come back to this momentarily. In Westfall, head for coordinates 37, 50 (you can see coordinates in the top right corner under your minimap, no add-ons required). Alliance can easily reach here from Stormwind as part of their normal questing journey, but Horde have a rougher time. Take the zeppelin from Orgrimmar to Stranglethorn Vale, then go north from Grom’gol through Darkshore and turn west when you can to Westfall. Beware, because Stranglethorn is full of high-level monsters that will aggro you if you breathe within a mile of them, and Darkshore and Westfall are full of Alliance NPCs. You can also swim the shore from Grom’gol up to the Westfall beach, if you prefer.

You’re looking to get to the middle of the Alexston Farmstead just southeast of the Gold Coast Quarry. There are a bunch of harvester enemies running around that may make things difficult, but if you can get clear of them you can interact with a Nailed Plank in a burnt-out cart. Alliance will pick up “…and that note you found” and Horde will get “Stepping Stones.”

Horde, you’ll start with this next step. Alliance, this is your step two. This one is in the Barrens. You’re looking for a burnt watchtower, at coordinates 46, 74 or so. Horde can get here easily by flying to Camp Taurajo (or walking from Orgrimmar, Crossroads, or Thunder Bluff) and taking the main road through the Barrens south. For Alliance, it’s a rougher journey, but you can make it by heading south from Darkshore (which is reachable by boat from Stormwind), through Ashenvale, and then down south further into the Barrens. At the watchtower, Horde will pick up the quest “…and that note you found” and Alliance will get “Stepping Stones.” Horde will then need to follow the previous step to Westfall to get their next quest.

Once you have “Stepping Stones,” the path is the same for both factions.

“Stepping Stones” takes you to Stonetalon Mountains, which Horde can get to from The Barrens and Alliance can get to…well, also from The Barrens, which is probably where you are if you just did the previous quest. Alliance have a hub at Stonetalon Peak, and Horde have Sunrock Retreat, but both groups will need to go past Sunrock Retreat and find a little path up into the mountains that lies just to the north of the outpost.

Follow the path carefully upward until you reach a small campsite with a fire, and a Pocket Litter you can interact with on top of a box. Finishing this quest will get you a 12-slot bag (yes!) and will let you pick up the next step, “Scramble.”

“Scramble”‘s turn-in point isn’t far away at all, but before you go, try to interact with the campfire. There’s a weird little quest you can do here called “Rekindle” that will restart the fire with the tinderbox and wood you got from the last quest. However, this quest was bugged for me when I did it and I was unable to click on the campfire, and this seems like a common problem a lot of people are experiencing. It will likely be patched in the future, but if it’s bugged when you reach it, don’t sweat it. You’re genuinely not missing any rewards and it’s not necessary to get the sleeping bag.

Campfire or no, head due north and up the hill, walking carefully so as not to fall down the cliff (if you do, no biggie, there’s a path that will let you climb back up easily). From the top you should be able to see the next objective, a Mound of Dirt, so jump over that way and turn in the quest, picking up “Wet job.”

Time to continent-hop again. You’re going back to Eastern Kingdoms, this time to Loch Modan. For Alliance, this is a short-ish run, and not a dangerous one. You can either start in Ironforge and walk south through Dun Morogh into Loch Modan, or go from Stormwind via boat at Menethil Harbor to Wetlands, and then had southeast through the mountain tunnel into Loch Modan.

Horde, this is another rough one. You’ll need to start in Undercity and run through Tirisfall Glades, exiting to the southwest into Silverpine Forest. Follow the path further south into Hillsbrad Foothills, continuing east into Arathi Highlands, across the southern bridge into Wetlands, and then finally through the mountain tunnel into Loch Modan. You will absolutely run into Alliance guards along the way and have to deal with PvP, there’s no way around it. Just corpse-run when you can and do your best.

Either way, you’ll want to end up at the Stonewrought Dam, which is at the very north end of the eponymous Loch of Loch Modan. You’ve got to climb atop the dam itself and walk across until you see a campsite of sorts on a ledge overlooking Wetlands. Once you’re in the right spot, descend onto the ledge above the stone heads and interact with the Eagle Figurine to complete your quest and pick up the next one, “Eagle’s Fist.”

Just one more step to go, and fortunately, it’s not too far away. Horde and Alliance alike will want to head north, back through Wetlands and Arathi Highlands toward Hillsbrad Foothills. On the border between Arathi and Hillsbrad is the Thoradin Wall, and this is your destination. Follow the wall north until you see a broken cart. The cart is on the Hillsbrad side of the wall, but this is a little easier to do at lower levels if you walk up the Arathi side and then go through the gap in the wall near the cart to cross over, as there are no monsters on the Arathi side.

You can use that cart to climb up the wall. There’s a bit of a platforming puzzle here. First climb on the weird cylinder thing, jump to the board that’s jutting out on the side, then up the cart to the wall. Then just follow the path you can take up the crumbling wall stones (start your climb on the low far left stone) until you see the camp ahead of you. Interact with the hanging Messenger Bag to finish “Eagle’s Fist” and pick up “This Must Be the Place.” Then, click on the Hastily Rolled-up Satchel to finish the last quest and get your sleeping bag at last. Congrats!

It's been a wild week for fans of the superhero genre. Yesterday the internet exploded when it was revealed that James Gunn and Peter Safran were stepping down as co-CEOS of DC Studios, and there are countless questions about how upcoming DC movies and shows will be affected. Some fan reacts are making me especially concerned about Lanterns (which is streaming with a HBO Max subscription) and more.

Gunn's tenure as DC's head has been cut short, and it's unclear if the first slate of projects called Gods and Monsters will still move forward. The director/writer/producer took to social media with a statement about his departure, and some of the responses on Threads are cutting me to the core. Case in point: the following response which has a whopping 1.8k likes.

Goddammit, we're never getting another Lanterns season are we?

Well, now I'm depressed. Ever since its first season ended, fans have been wondering if Lanterns would get a second season on HBO. After all, there's plenty more Green Lantern lore to explore, with the writer Venessa Baden Kelly interested in bringing in Kilowog to the series. Unfortunately, Gunn's departure might put the show's second season in jeopardy, especially after Lanterns was the subject of fan backlash.

This isn't the only depressing fan response to James Gunn's threads post. Another one that's hitting hard and has over 900 likes reads:

We're never getting a full DC run ever. 😭

Ouch. While the Marvel Cinematic Universe has become a well-oiled machine over its nearly two decades in theaters, the same can't be said for things at DC. The former DCEU began with Zack Snyder's movies, which quickly put the Justice League together rather than methodically giving them solo movies. Unfortunately that shared universe started becoming less and less interconnected over the years, eventually ending with Aquaman 2.

James Gunn and Peter Safran were hoping to make a more cohesive franchise with the DCU, and there were a number of thrilling crossovers in the first few titles. While we'll still get to see a number of characters collide when Man of Tomorrow hits theaters next summer, it's unclear exactly how the burgeoning shared universe will continue afterward. For hardcore superhero fans, it feels like we'll never get a DC counterpart to the MCU, which is super depressing.

Right now there are more questions about the DCU than answers. Gunn and Safran were replaced by former Marvel executive and producer Jeremy Latcham, who obviously has experience in the genre. We'll just have to wait and see what comes next.

The next DC movie hitting theaters is Man of Tomorrow on July 9, 2027. For now fans can see Clayface in theaters as part of the 2026 movie release list.

#3650. Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy, The Follow-Up To Rogue Trader, Gets Early 2027 Release Date

Warhammer: 40,000: Dark Heresy developer Owlcat Games has confirmed that the CRPG will officially launch on January 28, 2027, for PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S. A follow-up to the studio's previous—and lengthy—game, Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader, Dark Heresy will put players in the boots of an Inquisitor, one of the chosen few who work in the shadows to hunt down heretics and purge worlds of dark influences.

Set in the Calixis sector, players will start as lowly acolytes, forming a band of outcasts as they embark on their crusade to root out all evil. Owlcat Games says you can recruit colorful characters to your gang, including abhumans like Cogg, dangerous Psykers like Saro, Pariahs like Discordance, and, for a touch of extra heresy, even xenos like the mysterious Aeldari Corsair Laarthyr or the flesh-eating Kroot Ra’akhti.

Each companion brings unique skills to the battlefield, as well as advice for the various crimes that you'll investigate. Owlcat Games added that Inquisitors can choose how to handle the task, but each decision will have consequences that'll affect your journey. The game is also coming to Switch 2 eventually, and Owlcat Games says it'll share more details about that version later. If you'd like to dress up your PC in a grimdark aesthetic, you can browse this collection of high-resolution Dark Heresy wallpapers for your rig.
