#3649. It’s A Relief To Go Back To The Simple Joy Of Ocarina Of Time After A Decade Of Being Overwhelmed By Breath Of The Wild

The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the WildThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of TimeThe Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom

My friends, put the tomatoes down. I havenât even gotten to speak yet. I, like most people who own a Nintendo Switch 2 and are killing time until Grand Theft Auto 6 launches next week, am playing The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and Iâm having a pretty good time going back to a game that was once an elementary school obsession for me, especially because itâs been a long time since I really felt a constant sense of progression in a Zelda game after a decade of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

Yeah, the game is incredibly simple by modern standards, and Nintendo has done a lot to ensure that by making the game demonstrably easier in dozens of small ways that add up, but I think that relative simplicity is what draws me to it. Iâve been chipping away at the game in short sessions, usually finishing a temple or two before putting it down for the rest of the day, and the tangible feeling of momentum is what keeps me coming back to it just about every other evening at this point.

Over the years, especially with the rise of open-world games, I have identified that I am a goal-oriented person when it comes to how a video game can hold my attention. Thereâs just so much competition for whatever spare hours I have that if the bulk of my time playing a game is spent getting to the things I care about, I can lose interest fairly quickly. I want to see where the story goes, I want to reach the end of a quest line, and I loathe tedious open-world traversal more than most video game activities.Â

I canât entirely avoid open-world games in 2026, but if a game doesnât have a quick or engaging way to get around a giant map, it actively deters me from playing it. I often cite the Infamous series, with all its superpowered movement and interesting environmental interactions, as a great example of a game that makes its open-world map tolerable to me. A car or a horse is probably not going to cut it. There are exceptions from time to time, such as Cyberpunk 2077âs Night City entrancing me so much that Iâd gladly take in the view as I drove around on my motorcycle. But if I can help it, I want to spend my limited gaming time on things that arenât simply moving from one side of a giant space to another.

Breath of the Wild and its excellent sequel, Tears of the Kingdom do a lot to break up the tedium of simply moving through a space. The survival sim-esque friction and gizmo-building mechanics are brilliant evolutions of the original Zelda formula, and Nintendoâs ability to still draw water from the well of a decades-old franchise is commendable. I really enjoyed my time with both games, despite them grinding against a lot of my ingrained gaming sensibilities. The puzzles in the shrines, the constant feeling of discovery in its giant open world, and the colorful casts of weirdos and heroes you meet throughout the games maintain all that same Zelda spirit, but with a meaningful expansion of what a Zelda game looks like.Â

But man, is it a relief to go back to Ocarina of Time. I want puzzle-solving and discovery that I can get to quickly, that doesnât need me to meaningfully prep a survival bag so I can trek to the other side of the map while hoping my melee weapons can last me the whole trip, and what Ocarina is delivering feels downright breezy. Iâm sorry, Iâm sorry. I know itâs regressive of me to say Iâd like for the series to strip away all the cool things itâs done in the past nine years, but I havenât had a Zelda experience that feels like this in so long. The top-down 2D games are similar (at least those that came after the pretty open-ended and opaque original game), but they donât have the targeting and swordplay of the postâOcarina of Time era that rounds out the vision I have of what makes a 3D Zelda game.

I donât really hold any illusions that Zelda is going to go back to the structure of Ocarina of Time, but it is refreshing to be handed the tools I need to accomplish things without worrying that my weapon is going to break from battle damage or that Iâll run out of some vital consumable before I reach my goal. The Legend of Zelda is gonna be fine no matter where it goes moving forward, but for as dated and small in scope as Ocarina of Time might feel compared to Tears of the Kingdom, it sure does remind me that there was once a time when I didnât feel like I was fighting against the elements just to get to where I wanted to go.

A South Carolina man has been arrested after allegedly leaving his six-year-old daughter in line at Target at 1 AM to save his spot for Pokemon trading cards.

South Carolina Social Services have taken the girl into emergency protective custody, and Dooley was charged with unlawful conduct toward a child.

Pokemon trading cards remain incredibly popular, with interest surging this year specifically, as people hunt for rare cards and then try to flip them for profit.

#3643. PlayStation Cancels Fairgames After Years Of Silence

Another one of PlayStation’s live-service games has crashed and burned, asÂ Fairgames, the company’s online shooter that was being developed by first-party PlayStation developer Haven Studios, has been canceled.

As reported by Bloomberg, Haven Studios isn’t undergoing any layoffs as a result of the cancelation, as “the studio will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities,” according to a statement provided to the publication by PlayStation. The decision comes after Fairgames‘ recent playtest didn’t live up to Sony’s internal expectations.

âWhile the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set,â PlayStation executives Sean Decker and John Doyle wrote in an email to employees and verified by Bloomberg. âCombined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game.â

FairgamesÂ was initially announced back in 2023, and was originally being led by Jade Raymond, known as a producer of the earlyÂ Assassin’s Creed games. Raymond left Haven Studios in 2025, though the project quietly continued development. We really haven’t heard much about the game since it was initially unveiled.

Haven Studios was initially founded in 2021, and Sony acquired the company in 2022 before it had even put out a game. Now, it sounds like those who had been working onÂ FairgamesÂ will support the development of other games by PlayStation studios.

Fairgames is the latest in a long line of live-service disasters for Sony as the company continues to greenlight and then cancel its various attempts at forever games. Perhaps most famously, the company removed multiplayer shooter Concord from storefronts and then subsequently shut down its developer, Firewalk Studios.

Despite all this, Sony is still adamant that live-service games are an important part of PlayStation’s future.

#3642. Benito Skinner’s ‘Overcompensating’ Returns for Season 2: More Laughs, More Sex, More Gay

It’s been a year and a half since the first season of Benito Skinner’s Prime Video comedy series, Overcompensating, debuted, and a lot has changed for him in that time. For one, Skinner—also known as Benny Drama, his online alter ego—is blond now. It’s a change he says may be permanent or perhaps semipermanent. “It’s how I see myself—as a blond,” he tells me over Zoom. “So we’re going to keep going with it for a sec.”

But Skinner has transformed in much less superficial ways since the launch of his hit Amazon series, which is based on his experiences coming out as gay as a Georgetown undergrad. Equal parts raunchy and heartwarming, the first season follows Benny (Skinner), a closeted former high school football player who attempts to navigate the chaos of college, where he forms an unlikely bond with a fellow student named Carmen (Wally Baram).

Skinner shares that making the second installment of the series was “way more fluid, way less stressed.” As it should have been. The first season was a popular hit for the streamer (it has a 93% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes), hard-launching Skinner as an exciting new voice plucked from the internet and ready for prime time.

Benny and Carmen begin the season as enemies.

The second season, which Vanity Fair can exclusively reveal will debut on February 17, 2027, expands the world he created with new storylines for the supporting characters—and bigger stakes for Benny as he comes into his own with his sexuality. Benny navigates not only coming out to his sister, Grace (Mary Beth Barone), and his parents (Connie Britton and Kyle MacLachlan), but also his own sexual exploration—and all the awkwardness that comes with it.

So much of what made the first season a hit—the awkward comedy, the silly themed parties, the talking Megan Fox poster—returns, but this time many of the characters grapple with deeper issues. Yet Skinner felt lighter making the show this time around. “I think in season one, Benny is that stressed, so that kind of worked,” he says. “But in this one, we’re having more fun. He has some joy, so we can loosen up a little bit.”

Connie Britton, center, reprises her role as Benny's mom.

After Overcompensating premiered, Skinner was approached, he says, by “a few gays” who told him, “I thought it’d be gayer, the show.” He promises that the second season delivers just that: “We’re creeping out of the closet,” says Skinner.

In the first season, Benny is trying to find his place on campus while constantly living in fear that the people around him will discover he’s gay. He falls for a dashing British classmate named Miles (Rish Shah), only to find out he is straight and has kissed Carmen. The season ends with Carmen revealing that she has also slept with Grace’s boyfriend, Peter (Adam DiMarco), and in the final moments, Carmen accidentally lets slip in front of Grace that Benny is gay.

Skinner and Lukas Gage reunite in season two.

In the upcoming season, Benny heads back home with his sister for the start of Christmas break, struggling because he hasn’t yet come out to his family. “If season one was about friends, I think this season is about family, and trying to reintroduce yourself to your parents after starting to become yourself,” says Skinner. The way his father finds out about it makes for an especially tense moment, and Benny goes to great lengths (like joining the crew team) to mend that bond with his dad. “That relationship between gay men and father, I think, is always fraught and confusing,” he says. “I just wanted to make it as honest as possible.”

At the start of the new season, Benny and Carmen are at odds; Grace and her boyfriend, Peter, have broken up; and many of the characters are exploring those feelings of loneliness that can crop up in college. A handful of exciting new faces also join this season. Australian actor Aisha Dee (The Bold Type) plays a new student who becomes an instant It girl on campus. AnnaSophia Robb (The Carrie Diaries) joins as an intense coxswain (the one who does the yelling) on the crew team. And Tony-nominated stage actor Tom Francis (Sunset Boulevard) plays the captain of the team, serving as Benny’s newest love interest.

Peter (Adam DiMarco) is looking for his path forward.

For Skinner, the second season is about capturing the ups and downs of coming out. It’s not just one reveal and then you’re out of the closet and everything is better. “I get to be even more specific about coming out and also tell a story that I think I haven’t seen yet done in this way, which is the complication of coming out—how you can take 10 steps forward, a hundred steps back,” he says.

Benny joins the crew team, where he meets a new love interest (Tom Francis).

There’s also a lot more sex. “There are a couple scenes that are definitely going to be off-limits for the family,” Skinner says. But of course, in Overcompensating, the sex scenes aren’t always smooth sailing. “I think our show is about trying to be sexy and then it going wrong, or feeling like you start to come into yourself but you get made a fool,” he says.

Skinner adds the title of executive music producer to his résumé this season. “It feels like a return to my radio-DJ roots, and that feels right,” he says. There’s more Britney Spears and Charli xcx (who appeared in a cameo last season), and he wanted the show’s music to remain an important part of the world. He even wrote a letter to Coldplay when he wanted to use the band’s song “Fix You” in this new season. “I love doing the letters to these guys because I’m like, So is Chris Martin reading this? Is this sent by owl? What’s the vibe?” he says with a smile.

Overcompensating’s return will come almost two years after its debut, and Skinner, who says he always plans to keep this story set in the characters’ college years, wants to make the wait a little shorter next time. “I apologize to everyone that it took a while,” he says. “TV takes a long time, so I’m trying to go faster, but daddy has to write it.”

“I don’t want any of these characters to feel like we’re pandering to maybe what we think the internet will want,” says Skinner of crafting the second installment after a hit first season.

“What I wanted to do is surprise people with where we took it,” says Skinner of the new season, “and have them be like, ‘Oh, this isn’t what I asked for, but it is something kind of delicious and new.’”

#3641. DC Studios Is Getting A Marvel Veteran To Replace James Gunn And Peter Safran

DC Studios co-presidents James Gunn and Peter Safran have officially announced they'll step down, and Marvel veteran Jeremy Latcham will replace them. Gunn and Safran architected the new DC Universe of films and TV series, and they also had ambitious plans to expand the DCU into video games. Latcham is no stranger to superhero cinema, with credits on several of Marvel's biggest projects, including Spider-Man, Guardians of the Galaxy, and Avengers.

"Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker, Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface," Gunn and Safran wrote in a statement (via Variety). "We're immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow."

Following the relaunch of the DC Universe in film, Gunn later spoke about the potential of cross-platform storytelling, saying actors would portray their characters across all forms of media—including video games. "We have a couple of little DC games coming out. But we also have talked about–and in early stages of planning--some bigger things," Gunn said in 2025. "One thing in particular I’m excited about, but it does take time."

We never got to hear David Corenswet reprise his role as Superman in a video game, and since then, big changes have happened behind the scenes. Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery was approved earlier this year, leading to a merger between Warner Bros. Interactive (the WB division that publishes video games based on the company's IP) and Paramount Games Studio.

While the ambitious plans for the video game side of DC Studios never materialized, Gunn and Safran were still busy building a new DC Universe for the big and small screen. Three feature films were released--Superman, Supergirl, and Clayface--while the TV side saw multiple animated and live-action projects like Lanterns, Creature Commandos, and Peacemaker. Next year's big project is the Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow, which Gunn wrote and co-directed, and The People v. Gorilla Grodd is an upcoming series that will see Skyler Gisondo back as Jimmy Olsen.

On the video game side, Rocksteady is rumored to be working on a new single-player Batman game.

If your Steam account is at least nine years old, you should be good. Maybe.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In compliance with local laws, Steam rolled out age verification in Australia two months ago. Controversially, it was based on whether you owned a credit card, which many Australians do not. Overnight, Australians stopped being able to see games that are rated R18+ in the Steam store, like Doom, if they didn't have a credit card linked to their account.

Just as suddenly, Steam support has now updated how age verification works for Australians. Adding a credit card to your account still works, but additionally: "Steam will automatically consider your account age verified if it is at least nine years old and has had a consistent email address or billing information."

If you've moved house in the last nine years and let Steam know about it then your billing information won't have been consistent, so I sure hope you haven't changed both your email and physical address in that time.

Valve notes that it is aware this solution still isn't ideal for everyone: "We understand that not all Australians will be able to verify their age using our existing options. We are looking into other ways to comply with Australia's age verification rules while also limiting the data we collect and store from users."

Other storefronts provide alternative options like ID scans and face scans via digital age assurer Yoti. The Microsoft Store also takes your email account into consideration, via VerifyMy, the same assurer YouTube uses.

#3639. GTA 5’s Trevor Should Be In GTA 6 Sitting On The Toilet To “Pass The Torch,” Actor Says

Steven Ogg famously portrayed the wildcard character Trevor in Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 5, and he wishes Rockstar brought the character back for GTA 6.

Speaking to Principle Magazine, Ogg said it would have been a nice moment to "pass the torch" to have Trevor show up at the beginning of GTA 6 "sitting on the toilet" or doing some "weird thing" like walking around having something fall on his head, knocking him to the ground.

In short, Ogg said he wanted Trevor to have some kind of "acknowledgement" that Trevor's story is over and it's time for Jason and Lucia to take center stage in GTA 6. Ogg said it could have been a nice full circle moment because, in GTA 5, Trevor's first scene shows him bashing Johnny Klebitz from GTA 4.

"I’m not a fan of all of the reboots and the sequels. I don’t get the … the hunger for that, but there is, because it makes money and that’s why people do it," he said.

Ogg went on to say things have come so far since GTA 5, so he wanted to see how characters from GTA 5 could look in GTA 6, given the technical improvements from the past decade.

"So, I’d be curious. But you know, not my duck, not my bottle. Not my monkey, not my cage," he said.

Also in the interview, Ogg pushed back against the online theories that he is no fan of GTA and Trevor. He said he's always been proud of Trevor and proud of what Rockstar created. He doesn't play GTA 5, but he said people are out of line for taking his soundbites about GTA 5 and spinning them into a belief that he's no fan of GTA or his character. He acknowledged he didn't like how people would call him Trevor, and not Steven, in real life, though.

"That’s been all blown out of proportion. Or that I hate GTA and now I’m starting to embrace it more. No, it’s just early on, there was a lot of people calling me Trevor. And I’d be like, 'Well, my name is Steven,'" he said. "So I could never understand that. So it’s always like 'What’s your name, David? Okay, Nolan.' It doesn’t make sense if you know someone’s name and you’re calling them someone else’s name. I don’t get it. And I understand people associate with characters and connections," he said. "At these Comic Cons, they’re not Documentary Cons. So I couldn’t be these people. I mean, I couldn’t even be Trevor, because he’s a cartoon. Simon [from The Walking Dead] was a human on a TV show, at least. Yeah, it’s just one of those things. It’s like… [scratches head]. It’s like me calling you, you know, Barbara."

Trevor was one of the three playable characters in GTA 5, alongside Michael (Ned Luke) and Franklin (Shawn Fonteno). Ogg, in particular, landed some notable acting roles after GTA 5, appearing in the TV shows Better Call Saul, Snowpiercer, and Westworld, along with the films Emancipation and Unabomber.

Trevor was apparently going to be in more content for GTA 5, as Ogg said Rockstar canceled Trevor-centric DLC that would have featured a James Bond-like story. Rockstar reportedly canceled the DLC so it could instead focus more on GTA Online, which is known to basically print money.

GTA 5 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

#3638. You Can Play GTA 6 On A 13-Year-Old Xbox And It’ll Run At The Same Framerate As PS5 Pro

GTA 6PS5 ProXbox Cloud GamingXbox Series X/S

Grand Theft Auto 6 is only coming to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S at launch, but that doesn’t mean those consoles will be the only places to play it. Technically, fans who are still on Xbox One, which came out back in 2013, will also have a shot at exploring Rockstar Games’ latest version of Vice City thanks to Xbox Cloud Gaming.

Microsoft revealed the surprise last-gen perk in an update to its cloud gaming program this week. “Grand Theft Auto VI will be playable on day one through Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S, starting at 1am ET,” the company announced. “That means more players can experience one of the most anticipated games of the year on the consoles they already own. The game uses Xbox Series S graphics settings when cloud-streamed with Xbox Cloud Gaming.”

Series S graphics settings include the game running at a targeted 30fps framerate, the same as what will be available to players on Xbox Series X and PS5, as well as PS5 Pro. Sony’s more powerful hardware will still give players access to improved image quality with PSSR, but the game won’t run at 60fps anywhere, at least not at launch.

So what do you need in order to play GTA 6 on an Xbox One? Well, you’ll still need to own a digital copy of the game, which costs $80 and began pre-loading this week. You’ll also need access to Xbox Cloud Gaming, either via a Game Pass subscription or via Ã  la carte pricing. Ten hours of cloud gaming time in Vice City will cost Xbox owners $4.

What you won’t be able to do is stream GTA 6 to a mobile device or PC. Those options, which are a standard part of the rest of Xbox Cloud Gaming’s offerings, are excluded from the streaming agreement with Rockstar. It’s unclear if that’s a functionality that may be added sometime down the road after the game has been out for a while. GTA 6 will also support remote play on both Xbox and PS5, meaning you can stream it to other screens locally, including the PS Portal.

“Weâre excited to bring Grand Theft Auto 6 to more Xbox players at launch, and we will also be adding more titles from Rockstar Games to Xbox Cloud Gaming including Grand Theft Auto 5, Red Dead Redemption 2, and more in the coming months,” Microsoft added in today’s announcement.

I have no idea how many Xbox Ones are still out in the wild, or how many people may be tempted to blow the dust off of them instead of upgrading to a current-gen console. But given the ongoing price hikes for both the PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, it’s a really nice option for those who can’t otherwise afford to buy new hardware this fall for GTA 6.

#3636. Switch 2 Just Had Its Best Sales Week Of 2026, And It’s All Because Of Zelda

Nintendo just released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake for Switch 2, and the themed console that Nintendo debuted with the game has, perhaps unsurprisingly, sold incredibly well.

Circana's Mat Piscatella shared new data that confirms the Switch 2 just had its best sales week of 2026 so far, based on dollar sales, thanks to the 40th Anniversary Edition console. The $520 console launched on October 29, and Circana's reporting period for the week ended on October 31.

#3635. GTA 6 Preorder Numbers Are So Good, Even Take-Two Is Struggling To Believe Them

Grand Theft Auto 6 looks set to be the best-selling game of 2026, and even publisher Take-Two Interactive is surprised at just how big the demand for it has been ahead of launch. In its second-quarter fiscal year 2027 results, Take-Two was bullish on the sales numbers for the game, but it has only slightly adjusted its forecast for the financial year ending March 31, 2027.

"Preorders for Grand Theft Auto 6 are tracking far above our initial expectations, and we know that the numbers will speak for themselves soon enough," Take-Two said. Originally, the publisher had predicted to make $7.9 – $8.1 billion in its current financial year, and it has increased this figure to $7.98 – $8.18 billion. Speaking to GamesIndustry.Biz, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said the reason for the modest increase was due to GTA 6's launch being so close.

"[We cannot] disclose the numbers, but the point that we’re making is our prior expectations obviously were aligned with our guidance, and the preorders are far exceeding our original expectations," Zelnick said. "We’re maintaining our guidance, because the release is only 10 days away and we’ll know a lot more after the release. We’re just not updating our numbers right now because we are so close to the launch. However, preorders are far exceeding our expectations."

Back in August, a third-party research company estimated that GTA 6 had already brought in more than $400 million in revenue from 4.38 million preorders, and with its launch just days away, that figure has certainly grown even more. Take-Two had previously spoken about the unprecedented preorder numbers it was experiencing for the game--while not sharing any concrete numbers--and so far, it looks like the $100 edition is a very popular option. Experts also believe that the majority of preorders will come in the week before launch.

#3633. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Water Temple Walkthrough

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Well, you’ve made it. You’re finally at the most infamous dungeon in all of Zelda-dom, the Water Temple of Ocarina of Time. Good news for you: In the remake, this dungeon is far, far easier than it’s ever been. A few of the edges have been sanded down, the rooms all look far more distinct and memorable so it’s less of a mental maze, and the iron boots can be equipped and de-equipped simply by pressing down on the gamepad. Compared to the original, it’s a smooth ride. But still, this is one of the most involved dungeons in the game, so buckle on that Zora Tunic and let’s get swimming.

To enter the Water Temple, you need to be wearing (no, I wasn’t joking) the Zora Tunic, which you get by freeing King Zora from his ice block back in Zora Domain. To do that, you need Blue Fire in a bottle, which you obtain in the Ice Cavern as an adult. You’ll also need the Iron Boots from that same cavern. If you haven’t gotten that far yet, back yourself up and come back to this guide later.

Once you’re in the temple, remove your iron boots and float to the top. Run forward, and you’ll be in a big, open room with a bunch of doors on all four sides across four different floors, and water below you. I’m going to be referring to this as the “main hall” going forward. We’re going to be here a lot. I’ll also be referring to doors by floor and cardinal direction, so if you’re ever confused about what I’m talking about, open that map.

The first thing you’re going to do is slay that Blue Tektite in front of you. Sword, hookshot, whatever you like, just get it out of the way.

Next, you’re going to equip those Iron Boots, descend to the first floor, and head through the east door. Once you’re inside, remove the boots to float upward for a cutscene with your fiancee, Ruto. When it’s over, grab the Dungeon Map from the chest in front of you, and then stand on the platform with the Triforce symbol and play Zelda’s Lullaby to lower the water level.

Real quick tip: There are three different spots to mess with the water level in this dungeon, and each one will raise it to a different spot. This one brings it down to the first floor, and is marked by glowy blue pillars. It might be good to make a note somewhere of which color results in which water level, just in case you ever get turned around or confused and the water level is in the wrong place.

Once the water has dropped, fearlessly jump down the hole, landing in the water below so it doesn’t damage you. Now, with the water taken care of, note that one of the torches in here is lit. Stand behind it with your bow equipped and aim an arrow through the fire to each of the two torches on the other end of the room to open the door in front of you, then enter. Defeat the three Spikes by blocking their attacks with your shield and swinging your sword when they’re vulnerable to obtain a Small Key. (Din’s Fire is also usable for this puzzle).

Backtrack the way you came in and head out into the main hall. There are two more aptly named Spikes out here waiting for you; get rid of them. To your left (west side, 1F) is a bombable/breakable wall. Knock that out, and use your Iron Boots to sink, sink, sink. Head down the underwater corridor and take care of the Shell Blade by hitting it with your hookshot when its mouth is all the way open. At the end of the corridor, take off the boots and rise up.

In here, climb the platform jutting out of the water and use the hookshot to grapple onto the pillars ahead of you. Take down the Tektites and the Like Like (Hookshot is great here), and you’ll be rewarded with the Compass. Now, all the way back to the main hall!

To the west (1F) is a block you can push forward until it drops in the water. Do that, then use the boots to sink again. Look out for the Shell Blade in the way, then rise back up at the end of the hall. You’ll find yourself in a room with a whirlpool and some statues underwater, and a chest on the other side.

This looks trickier than it is. Use the iron boots to drop into the whirlpool, aiming for the center platform (the serpent’s body) stretched down the middle of the pool. Stand on the platform and use your hookshot to smack the weird gem thing in the serpent’s mouth. This will unlock the underwater grate, allowing you to enter. You might need to don and doff the iron boots a few times to swim over properly, but with some careful aiming it’s very doable. There are two more Shell Blades to fight inside, after which you’re free to take off the boots, rise to the surface, and grab the small key.

Back across the whirlpool, out the door, into the main hall again. There’s a locked door on the central pillar here, directly in front of you, and you now have a key. Head inside.

Once inside, step forward, turn around, and look up for a grapple point. Use your hookshot to get on the platform above. Right in front of you is a spot to stand and play Zelda’s Lullaby to raise the water back up. (Note: the columns here are green, green brings the water to 2F! Write it down if you need to!) Before you leave this inside pillar, though, jump in the water and look down: a new gap has opened up with the water level rising.

Use iron boots to drop down, where three Spikes are waiting for you. Kill them with the hookshot, then use the hookshot to hit the green switch above your head, releasing a Shell Blade. Kill that too, then remove the iron boots where it was standing to rise up into the now-open area. There’s a red rupee in a chest on the way up, as well as a gold skulltula on the wall opposite. Funny, I feel like something else used to be here in the original game…anyway, grab these, backtrack the way you came in, and take off the boots to rise back up into the middle of the pillar. Then swim out the door into the main hall.

Directly in front of you across the water (2F, east side) is a bombable/hammerable wall in an alcove. You know what to do. Smash the pots for bombs if needed, otherwise use the Megaton Hammer if you’ve cleared the Fire Temple already, and head on through.

Be cautious as you head into the water and equip the Iron Boots. There are four Stingers waiting for you. Your hookshot will take care of them, but it’s easy to get overwhelmed, so take it slow (not that you can do otherwise with those boots on). Once they’re dead, proceed to the end of the underwater hallway and unequip the boots to rise to the surface.

In front of you is a pool of water with a switch in it, and a round platform being lifted by a fountain. Use your hookshot to hit the switch to lower the platform, stand on the platform, then use hookshot again on the same switch to raise yourself up to the floor above. Your reward is a Small Key. Take it, then backtrack all the way to the main hall again.

In the main hall, hop in the water and swim around the central pillar to the locked door directly across from where you just entered. It’s got glowing red columns around itâcan’t miss it. Use the Small Key and head inside. Smack the switch and ready yourself; a blue Tektite will descend and try to fight you. Once it’s dispatched, stand on the lowered platform and use your hookshot to hit the switch again and rise up.

It’s another Zelda’s Lullaby spot, this time with red lights, that will bring the water to 3F! Play that same song! Up goes the water. Jump down from the ledge next to the Triforce symbol and back into the water of the main room.

Mind any Tektites you haven’t dispatched already and swim on over to 3F, west side, for another locked door for which you conveniently have a key.

A couple of Keese will be waiting for you to slash them up. Take stock of your surroundings before you proceed. You’ll want to use the hookshot to grapple your way up these moving platforms to the top, one by one. Start by dropping down to the platform below the one you start on, and it’ll descend until you can grapple across. Then just work your way up, one by one. Don’t panic, it’s very doable, and there’s a stable platform to the side you can jump to if you need a second to collect yourself. Head through the door at the top once you reach it.

In this next room, I started by hitting all the Tektites below with my arrows just to get them out of the way. Then, use your hookshot to hit the switch at the center of the room and make the grapple points raise up. You’ll want to grapple to the first point directly in front of you, then (counterintuitively) hit the switch again to lower the points. Use the grapple point on the next wall to crossâyou’ll be able to continue along the ledge only if the grapple point pillars are lowered. Hit the switch yet again and grapple to the final pillar, hit the switchÂ again to lower the pillars. Climb atop the one next to you, then hit the switch one final time to raise the pillar and lift you within reach of the next floor.

Hit those pots for health, arrows, whatever before you go through the door, it’s time for one of the best bosses in the game!

Shadow Link is tough; he mirrors your moves! Don’t attack him head-on while his shield is up or he’ll do something I hear the kids call “aura farming.” I was able to beat him pretty easily by keeping my guard up and dodging his combos, waiting for an opening. In the first phase of the fight, I would dodge to the left side twice whenever he swung, then would come in for a combo toward his exposed back. In the second phase, this was trickier, but still very doable if I dodged backwards twice and then threw out the hookshot to stun him. Make sure you dodge backwards far enough when he gears up for a spin attack, and don’t let yourself get pushed too close to the arena walls, or he can pin you down for some big damage.

With Shadow Link down, head through the door opposite where you came in (use your map if you got turned around) to finally obtain the Longshot, which will let you hookshot targets even farther away than before! To escape this room, aim for the very far away targets above you, then drop down the waterfall into the cavern below. Let yourself float down the river, but mind the whirlpoolsâyou can use the iron boots to just walk between them underwater. About three-quarters of the way down the river, there’s a gold skulltula on a wall above you. Make sure you’re firmly iron-booted underwater, then use the longshot to smack it once to defeat it, and then again to collect the token.

Climb atop the stone outcropping on the end of the river and use the longshot again, once to hit the eye above the gates and open them, and again to grapple to the grapple point on the other side of the gates before they close on you.

We’re back in familiar territory, so head out to the main hall once again. We’ve still got some work to do, and we’re sorely in want of a boss key right about now. First, we need to get the water level down. Get those boots on and drop down to 1F east, the room where you first ran into Ruto. Swim up to the Triforce and play Zelda’s Lullaby to drop the water, then head back into the main hall. Then, you want to enter the central pillar again from the door on 1F. We’re here to raise the water level, but hold up. Grapple to the Triforce stand, then look at the ceiling for a grapple point you can now reach with the longshot. Fly on up there, then look across to the other side of the ceiling for another gold skulltula. Once you have that, drop back down and play Zelda’s Lullaby.

Everything’s in place! Exit the pillar and run around the central platform to stand on the floating block, looking across at the outer wall. You should see a gate with a grapple point on the other side, and an eye switch above. Once again, use the longshot to hit the eye, then immediately use it again on the grapple to get through. Drop into the pool and equip the iron boots, then walk into the hallway. There’s a movable block wedged into the wall hereâpull it out as far as you can, blocking off the hallway, then take off the boots and swim up and out of the pool. You should be able to see a fence ahead of you with a waterfall on the other side, and a grapple point on the ceiling. Grapple to it with the longshot, use the iron boots to sink into the water, then head down the hallway and push the block out of your way to clear a path to the chest with yet another small key.

Back to the main hall again, equipping the iron boots again and sinking down to 1F, north. Grapple across the gap and use your small key on the door. Inside, there are a lot of tektites in the way. Use your sword, shield, bow, whatever, to get them out of the way (seriously, they will knock you into whirlpools otherwise). Carefully cross the room, avoiding the boulders, using the iron boots as needed to stay out of whirlpools, and go through the door. In here, use the longshot to dispatch all the stingers, then smash the rock walls (with bombs or the megaton hammer) to reveal a block that can be pushed into the water to hit a switch. The switch will raise the water level for you to head out the door in the wall above.

Whew. Almost done. In here, step on the switch to raise platforms you can jump across, and a tektite with them. Get rid of it (and the other tektite on the other side of the room) as you see fit, then cross and go through the opening. On the other side, be careful. Boulders are rolling down this stream and will run you over if you step in at the wrong time. Wait for one to pass, then go under the waterfall and immediately turn to the left to jump into the alcove. There’s a shell blade waiting, so get that out of the way. Before you head through the door, turn back, wait for the boulder to pass, then jump back in the stream, through the waterfall, and look upâthere’s another gold skulltula near the ceiling. Grab it fast, then turn back and head through the door to, at long last, claim the boss key.

Great work, folks! Turn back, follow the boulders down the stream and into the room you were in earlier with the boulders and whirlpools, then back into the main hall. I’m sorry to say we’ve got to mess with the water levels one more time. You’ll need to go back into 2F west, head up the fountain, and play Zelda’s Lullaby one last time to raise the water and open a path up the big stairs to the north on 2F (technically 3F). Drop down, and head that direction. You’ll have to stand on the platform of the central pillar and longshot your way over. Load up on hearts from the pots before you go in, and get ready to fight.

Okay, not yet. Use your iron boots in this room to climb the waterfall and avoid the spiky things spinning back and forth.Â Now get ready to fight!

Morpha isn’t too bad, as bosses go. The boss itself is the weird red Metroid-looking ball thingie that’s hiding in the tentacles. Your main goal is to use the longshot to rip it out of its watery protection and whack it a bunch with your sword. This is pretty easy with Navi’s targeting; the main thing you need to worry about is getting hit by water tentacles. Morpha will manifest these out of the water and try and slam them on the ground near you. Early on, they’ll be pretty spread out, but later in the fight they’ll form a big wall that’s harder to avoid. If you get trapped you can also use the grapple points on the sides of the room to fly out of danger. I tried to stay on the edges as much as possible; you never really want to be in the water with Morpha. But you can use the central platforms to bait Morpha into an easier spot for you to longshot the ball out, or just to cross out of the way of attacks. Try to be aware of where Morpha the Ball is at all times, as this fight can get annoying if it’s always all the way across the room, just out of range. Use those grapple points!

That’s the Water Temple done, folks! Enjoy the cutscenes, and get the heck outta there to see how the Zora are doing.

Oh, psst. Once the cutscenes are over, you’ll be at Lake Hylia, just before sunrise. Check out the stone monument in front of you to make good use of that timing. You’re welcome!

Take-Two Interactive, the publisher, recently shared that another 5 million copies of GTA 5 were sold in the past 90 days during its second-quarter fiscal year 2027 update.

Whether GTA 6 will surpass these numbers is still unknown, but Take-Two Interactive is optimistic as preorders for the November 19 launch are already higher than expected.

#3631. Nintendo’s New Gift-Giving Feature Comes With Some Very Nintendo Restrictions

A new update is available for all Nintendo Switch 2 and Switch consoles, and if you're on a Nintendo Account family plan, version 23.5.0 will allow you to once again gift games to members in your group.

"Just in time for the holidays, a new feature will let family group members gift digital games to other members of their group," Nintendo wrote in an update. "You will be able to gift digital products that you purchase through Nintendo eShop on your device to family group members. This includes eligible games as well as DLC and upgrade packs."

In typical Nintendo fashion, what should be a straightforward program does have some strange restrictions. The company has noted that not every item is eligible for digital gifting and that the number of digital gifts handed out within a specific period is limited. This isn't the first time that Nintendo has offered a digital gifting program, as way back in the Wii era, owners of the console could visit the Wii Shop and grab some WiiWare or Virtual Console games. From there, users were free to gift them to anyone on their Wii friend list. That service was eventually closed after the Wii Shop Channel was shut down in 2019.

To gift someone in your family group a game, you'll need to visit the Nintendo eShop on your Switch console, find the product page, and select the "Give as a Gift" box before you check out. Select the lucky recipient, complete your purchase, and they'll receive a nice little surprise.

In related Nintendo news, the Switch 2 just had its best sales week of 2026, thanks to one plucky console dressed in green. The launch of the limited-edition Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2 console--which costs $520 and doesn't include a copy of the Zelda game it's inspired by--proved to be easy money for Nintendo, as it contributed to an 81% total hardware spend increase in the US for the week, compared to the same week in 2025. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake also launched last week, and it's currently the highest-rated game of 2026.

#3630. Student Game Development Competition Shut Down Because Kids Kept Submitting AI Slop

This will be the last year for the Australian STEM Videogame Challenge, a competition for young people, as the entries have grown overrun with AI-generated slop. According to a report in PC Gamer the event, which has been around for 12 years, will cease operations because it was getting too difficult to determine which games were made with AI and which were made entirely by the kids themselves.

The contest was open to students from elementary to high school, and required kids either working alone or in groups of up to four people to submit a game based on a chosen theme complete with a design document and a short trailer showing off the game. On Reddit, a parent of a child who regularly submitted games to the competition lamented the competition’s shutdown. “My teenage son and his friends entered the competition for several years, meeting up regularly, discussing ideas, and working together on a shared passion project,” the parent wrote. “It gave them something exciting to work on, and a common goal to strive towards outside of school. It also gave them confidence, and made them feel part of a wider community.”

In a statement to PC Gamer, Cathy Zemaitis, head of the Student Learning and Progress division at ACER, the company that puts on the challenge, said, “The decision was driven by the rapid and complex rise of generative AI in game development, making it harder to judge what students made themselves, and moving the program away from its original purpose.”

The “justification” for using AI in a professional game development setting is to essentially make games faster and more cheaply. One of the stated purposes of the challenge is to “enable students to develop real-world skills.” How is that accomplished using AI tools, especially at an age when core game development skills haven’t yet been learned? I’d imagine not very effectively. And it really sucks that the example adults are setting with the push for and normalization of generative AI is resulting in the end of a valuable opportunity for the next generation to develop a skill. We are eating the game development seed corn.

“I know as adults the world can be unfair, and we need to adapt,” the parent on Reddit wrote. “But this really hit home for me, because the victims this time are children. My son was visibly gutted when I told him the news, and it genuinely felt like part of his identity had been destroyed.”

#3629. Big Walk’s AI Usage Was Tiny, But Its Disclosure Has Sparked A Bigger Debate

Big Walk developer House House has confirmed that it used AI during the "final stretch" of its development. The studio recently updated its FAQs page to confirm its use of the tech, with the news coming after 19 Independent Games Festival jurors announced they'll decline to vote for "any game that uses generative AI in any capacity" during the 2027 awards show.

House House hasn't confirmed if its admittance was connected to the IGF--the IGF hasn't named any games either--and the studio said to Aftermath that it estimates "that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code" was built with AI. "We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalization of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable.' We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologize that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards," House House said. The developer also mentioned that AI was used as a last resort for solving technical issues, as even an engineer at Unity--the engine that Big Walk was developed in--believed that one of their problems wasn't possible to solve.

There's a lot to unpack here, starting with why House House didn't disclose the use of AI for Big Walk. The game is hosted on platforms like Steam, where studios can voluntarily disclose AI usage when it comes to generated code (however, it is mandatory to disclose if a game has AI-generated assets), but House House says it only did so after the topic became a matter of public interest. It also added that it will continue to support developers looking to limit "the harm generative AI is doing to video games and our world."

Pathologic 2 localization writer Bruno Diaz also touched on the controversy, explaining that IGF rules required studios to disclose the use of AI in development. Game designer Austin Walker posted online that the IGF committee has been debating the use of AI in game development, leading 19 jurors to issue a statement. While the group says it doesn't speak for the entire IGF organization or all jurors involved in the IGF Awards, IGF leadership supports the statement. Overall, if AI is used in any part of a game's development, from coding to visual assets, the jurors will not vote for it.

"Programming is a creative discipline whose labor deserves the same respect we extend to any part of making a game," the IGF juror's statement reads. "This extends to the past work used to train these models without the creators' consent."

The IGF's stance comes as the discussion over AI heats up in the games industry. Proponents argue it'll make video game development faster and more affordable; others argue it contributes to environmental harm and is leading to job losses across multiple fields. Others have argued that House House's use of AI to solve challenging coding bugs isn't a big deal, but critics say the AI disclosure should have been there from the beginning.

At the same time, the frequency of AI slop games has exploded in recent months, with the October edition of Steam Next Fest being a dumping ground for hastily vibe-coded game demos. Copycats have also become a major headache, with several game developers withdrawing their demos from the public over fears that bad actors will copy their work and rush a clone to market.

Rockstar has finally shared details on what PlayStation 5 Pro owners can expect from Grand Theft Auto 6 on their expensive consoles, but has also confirmed that all platforms will run at the exact same frame rate.

PlayStation 5 Pro players can look forward to PSSR support, which will use Sony's well-tuned upscaler to provide a cleaner image compared to that on the base PS5. GTA 6 is available to pre-load now across all release platforms, with some already reporting that GTA 6's story is appearing as a separate download, fuelling speculation that a new online mode isn't that far away. There are a lot of upcoming Hallmark movies to look forward to, especially as Countdown to Christmas continues. Many of these films are led by Hallmark staples, of course, but it’s hard not to think about previous network stars who used to headline those offerings. This includes Danica McKellar, who is one of many ex-Hallmark stars to have joined rival company GAF. However, the Wonder Years alum is speaking out about the whole situation and wants fans to know she didn’t leave.

In 2021, McKellar exited Hallmark after signing a multi-picture deal with Great American Family. Over her six-year tenure at Hallmark, McKellar starred in nearly 20 films, so it was definitely a shock when her departure was confirmed. However, McKellar recently clarified the situation and made note of how Bill Abbott -- the former president and CEO of Hallmark Channel’s parent company, Crown Media -- factored into it. She told PauseRewind via Komo News:

I don't feel like I left. I feel like I stayed with the person and he has just given me so much more creative freedom.

Abbott was the president and CEO of Crown Media for 11 years before ultimately starting GAF. Considering their prior working relationship, it's admittedly understandable that McKellar would want to follow him to a new network. And, of course, the desire for more creative freedom is also reasonable for an actor.

So, from McKellar's point of view, she didn’t “leave” Hallmark but simply stuck with the person who helped build the network amid his venture into something new. As for how her new work situation is going, McKellar notes that she’s much more involved at GAF when it comes to making her movies. Overall, it sounds like the former child star has been relishing that:

I’m involved in rewrites for sure on the script. I help casting. I help make decisions about props. Sometimes I buy my own wardrobe or props because I'm like, oh, this would be perfect and they're always so receptive, which is great. And I'm very involved in the edit, choosing music, all that kind of stuff.

McKellar’s feelings about having creative control and being more involved are similar to what Candace Cameron Bure has said about GAF. The Full House alum, who also made the switch from Hallmark in 2022, has opened up about living her dream making faith-centered movies. She serves as an executive producer on all of her GAF films and even some films she doesn’t appear in. It definitely seems like both McKellar and Bure are a lot more hands-on than they were at Hallmark.

Even though McKellar is no longer on the network, she has no problem defending her Hallmark movies either. They’ve gotten a bad rap over the years, with many pointing out that Hallmark movies are far too predictable and the network hasn’t embraced POC and LGBTQ+-centric stories. However, the cable channel has been working to make some changes over the years, and McKellar still shows her support to her Hallmark friends and their movies.

While I miss seeing Danica McKellar on her previous network, I can’t say I blame her for being content at Great American Family. It's my hope that she continues to headline entertaining films that delight audiences whether they arrive during the holidays or not. On that note, though, with the holiday season coming up, there are going to be a lot more Christmas movies to look forward to that aren’t just on Hallmark.

#3626. Here’s How Your Xbox One Can Play GTA 6

Grand Theft Auto 6 is out next week, and the game is launching on both Xbox Series X|S and PS5. If you don't have an expensive current-generation system, it previously appeared you would be out of luck to play GTA 6, but that's not the case.

Rockstar officially confirmed on November 10 that Grand Theft Auto 6 will support Xbox Cloud Gaming. This feature allows you to stream the game to Xbox Series X|S or Xbox One, and uses Xbox Series S graphics settings. This means it'll look a little worse than running it natively on the Xbox Series X, but if you are still rocking with an Xbox One, this is the only way you can play the game.

"And as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay," Rockstar added in its announcement.

The catch to all this, outside of the game unlocking an hour later than the native versions, is that Microsoft just so happened to add a time limit to Xbox Cloud Gaming starting in November. If you have a Game Pass Ultimate subscription, you can play 15 hours a month via Xbox Cloud Gaming. Those without a subscription can buy time, as well, but 50 hours will cost $12, and that's on top of the cost of Grand Theft Auto 6 itself.

GTA 6 officially launches November 19. It will also support Remote Play across both PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and includes some bonus performance features for PS5 Pro. Though the game will be single-player at launch, some files seem to suggest multiplayer is on the way.

#3625. Johnny Depp on Honoring Hunter S. Thompson’s Final Wish With a “Death Cannon” That Stood “Taller Than the Statue of Liberty”

He couldn’t remember if it was day or night when he found it, in the place where “one never quite knew or cared for time,” Johnny Depp wrote. He remembered the year—1997—and that he was with Hunter S. Thompson in his basement War Room at Owl Farm. It was just across the hall from Depp’s bedroom, with that old keg of dynamite serving as his bedside table.

Rummaging through beaten-up boxes that comprised Thompson’s archive, Depp unearthed something that would turn out to be equally explosive. “A battered typescript,” he called it. Abandoned among the detritus of Thompson’s renegade life, it was “bound together by rubber bands.” On its cover, “in Hunter’s own hand,” Depp noted, were the words THE RUM DIARY.

“He wrote the book in his early twenties,” Depp wrote. “And then stuffed it away.”

Side by side on the floor of the War Room, Depp and Thompson began “reading it to one another.” And when they were done, Depp had made a decision: “The Rum Diary was simply too good to remain lost.”

Thompson wasn’t able to find a publisher for The Rum Diary when it was written, but now he was, well, Hunter S. Thompson. With Depp as his advocate, The Rum Diary was published in 1998. “Almost immediately, the subject of a film was broached,” Depp wrote in a foreword to the screenplay, recalling Thompson saying, “‘Hot damn . . . yessir, let’s you and I produce this caper together, Colonel! We’ll have Hollywood groveling at our feet! They will crawl over a road of bones to get to us! Yessir!’”

A movie didn’t happen “as easily as we had hoped,” Depp continued in his foreword. “Fiery hoops of all dimensions, covert bear traps, woefully obstinate billfolds” arose in their path, “which neither Hunter or I were remotely experienced in battling . . . But we weren’t giving up.”

Hunter S. Thompson at his ranch in Colorado, 1990.

As the years wore on, Thompson grew increasingly inflamed over the development hell of Hollywood, writing producer Holly Sorensen a fiery missive in January 2001: “Dear Holly, Okay, you lazy bitch, I’m getting tired of this waterhead fuckaround that you’re doing with The Rum Diary. We are not even spinning our wheels aggressively. It’s like the whole Project got turned over to Zombies who live in cardboard boxes under the Hollywood Freeway. I seem to be the only person who’s doing anything about getting this movie Made. I have rounded up Depp, Benicio del Toro, Brad Pitt, Nick Nolte and a fine screenwriter from England named Michael Thomas.”

The eventual screenwriter for The Rum Diary turned out to be Bruce Robinson, the British director of the twisted 1987 cult classic Withnail and I, which both Depp and Thompson were “mutually obsessed with.” Depp had originally asked Robinson to direct the film adaptation of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas—but by then, Robinson had quit directing, wrung out by the Hollywood system that had subjected him to making the Uma Thurman–led thriller Jennifer 8 for Paramount. He was content to spend the rest of his life writing screenplays and books and had vowed to never direct a movie again.

In 2005, Johnny tracked Robinson down while he was on vacation in Spain. “Have you read The Rum Diary?” Depp asked. Bruce hadn’t. The next day there was a knock on Robinson’s hotel room door, along with “the book The Rum Diary that Johnny had sent,” said Robinson.

“I wasn’t impressed by the book,” he continued. Neither were most critics: “For someone who gets to drink rum all day and have sex on the beach (the real thing, not the cocktail) all night, Kemp is pretty morose,” wrote one reviewer of the Thompson character. Despite some early incantations of the hellish voice that Thompson used with such tremendous force later in his career, it had many of the problems that plague early attempts at fiction. But because it was Johnny Depp, Robinson said he would try his hand at writing the screenplay.

Once back in Herefordshire, however, he found he could not write. Not a single word. “Nothing, nothing, nothing,” he said.

He knew the problem: abstinence. “I think it’s called alcoholism, probably,” he said of his tolerance for red wine. He had been sober for six and a half years, before which he had been “literally drinking wine all day while I worked. I’d finally gotten to the point where I was tired of doing that every day, seven days a week, so I cut the booze out of my life completely.”

Now he was stuck. Without the wine, which he said unleashed him from the gridlock of his superego, he was blocked. “You know I’m just going to have to drink some wine for this,” he finally confided to his wife. With her blessings, he opened a bottle of red, and then another and another, “one bottle of red wine a day—every day—for the three months it took me to write the story,” he said.

Then, as he was almost done with the screenplay (along with the Bordeaux), he drove into town to get the Sunday papers. The news was all over his radio: the American writer and journalist Hunter S. Thompson had killed himself.

“Oh, my God,” Robinson thought. “That’s the end of the movie.”

Hunter S. Thompson takes on his ranch in Colorado, 1976

Sunday, February 20, 2005. A heavy rainstorm lashed the streets of Los Angeles. Mist clung to the palms and a sense of gloom fell over the city, as it always does when it rains in L.A. Christi Dembrowski turned off Sunset and drove up the winding road to her brother’s home, bearing news that she knew would break Johnny’s heart: Hunter S. Thompson had died that afternoon of a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head.

“My sister Christi turned up at the house in a pouring rainstorm,” Depp said. “She’d received a phone call two hours after it had happened and didn’t want me to see it on CNN. She told me Hunter had gone. But as much of a shock as it was, as much horror as I felt when you receive such blunt, bad news, I also knew Hunter was never going to be the guy who was going to collapse in a bowl of soup.”

After the shock—along with the eulogies for the fallen writer dominating airwaves, telephone lines, and barrooms worldwide—came what Depp called the “devastation.”

“Tragic,” he told Tom Thurman in the 2006 documentary Buy the Ticket, Take the Ride: Hunter S. Thompson on Film. “Shocked but not shocked. Angry but understanding. A zillion different emotions flying around all the time. It was like somebody had removed something from your body. It was a heavy hit.”

Mourning the loss of his brother, mentor, hero, and friend, Johnny’s mind flashed back to the 1978 BBC documentary Fear and Loathing in Gonzovision, in which Thompson described in minute detail how he would like to be sent off from this world into the next: he wanted his remains cremated and shot from a cannon on his land in Woody Creek, Colorado.

“When I got the news that Hunter had made his exit, obviously I was devastated,” Depp said. “I remember thinking almost immediately, ‘The cannon. We’ve got to do the cannon.’”

For Depp, this wasn’t a writer’s fantasy; it was Thompson’s final command. “That bastard,” Depp said. “I know somewhere in his crooked mind . . . he knew that I was the only one perhaps loyal enough, perhaps insane enough, to attempt it.”

Over the years, Thompson had spoken about what would be called “the death cannon,” Depp said. “You know, he brought it up every now and again; ‘Oh, yeah, I’ve got to have—I need the cannon, you know. . . . I may have even said, ‘I’ll send you off.’”

Thompson’s son, Juan, was determined to make it happen, too. Only Juan envisioned a twelve-foot cannon, costing a couple of hundred dollars. Johnny wanted something bigger, grander. “A few days later, Doug Brinkley, Hunter’s good friend and editor of his letters books, came over to our cabin and said Johnny Depp had called and said he wanted to pay for the construction of the cannon,” Juan wrote in his 2016 memoir Stories I Tell Myself: Growing Up with Hunter S. Thompson. “We were astonished . . . it is one thing to be a friend; it’s another thing to volunteer to build a friend’s death cannon.

An initial commemoration of Thompson’s life was held at the Hotel Jerome in Aspen on March 5, 2005. It was “essentially a party with music, photos and videos, interspersed with testimonials from friends and family,” Juan wrote. Depp flew to Aspen with Benicio del Toro and John Cusack to attend it. During the event, one of Depp’s assistants found Juan in the crowd “and asked me to come with him to Johnny’s room,” Juan wrote.

The assistant “slowly opened the door. And I entered the dark room and looked around, and in the center of the bed was a sculpture, lit from within. A giant boom box was playing Norman Greenbaum’s “Spirit in the Sky,” with its lyrics, “When I lay me down to die / Goin’ up to the spirit in the sky.”

“The sculpture was a tapering silver tower made of aluminum, about three feet high, topped by a blood-red fist,” Juan remembered. “The two-thumbed fist. The peyote button glowed from within with shifting colors. There was a small hole in the top of the fist where the projectile would exit.”

It was a magnificent miniature model that exceeded even Hunter Thompson’s wildest dreams. The full version, as envisioned by Johnny, would be “153 feet tall, 15 stories, taller even than what Hunter imagined,” wrote Juan. “Taller than the Statue of Liberty.”

The cannon would be fabricated in Los Angeles and hauled in pieces to Owl Farm on flatbed trucks. “It has to be perfect,” Depp told his long-time contractor, Steve Cohn, who coordinated the event over three months in Aspen (residing in three suites in three different Aspen hotels; at one of them, the Sky Hotel, Cohn allegedly set the record on room service booze and “incidentals,” spending more than $100,000). No expense was spared for what would become a monumental undertaking, requiring six months of massive set designing, and construction and engineering crews “numbering at least a hundred” from Hollywood and beyond, said Cohn.

On August 20, 2005, a crowd of 250, including Jack Nicholson, Sean Penn, Bill Murray, and Senators George McGovern and John Kerry, assembled on the meadow behind Thompson’s home. After the toasts and speeches (“Hunter, this is for you,” said Depp), a video clip of Thompson discussing his funeral cannon in his 1978 BBC interview was played on a giant screen. A Japanese drum ensemble began performing. Glasses of champagne were passed around. Then all eyes were on the massive cannon, its red fabric curtains unfurling to reveal the gonzo logo—the two-thumbed fist and the pulsating green peyote button—at the top of the 153-foot tower. “Spirit in the Sky” blasted from the speakers. “Then, at 8:46 p.m., more than thirty fireworks rocketed high above Owl Farm . . .” Doug Brinkley wrote in Rolling Stone. “The cannon atop the tower fired, and Hunter’s ashes fell over the assembled guests like gray snow. ‘Mr. Tambourine Man’ blaring from the sound system on cue. Hunter was literally all around us now. . . . ‘I have never seen an event like this,’ whispered the actor Harry Dean Stanton. ‘And I’m old. Very old.’”

“Everybody was speechless,” said Cohn. “Johnny and I were sitting together when it went off. He looked at me, smiled, and said, ‘That was awesome.’”

With Thompson’s ashes in the air, the party began in a massive tent decorated to look like Hunter’s kitchen and living room.

Bruce Robinson’s initial thought was that the death of Hunter Thompson would mean the death of The Rum Diary. But he was wrong about that.

“I had lost my dear friend and co-conspirator,” Depp wrote. “Sure as fuck wasn’t going to give up now.”

#3624. Sony Is Bringing The Best Trend Of ’90s Console Design To PS5

Sony is embracing one of the best trends of the late '90s and early 2000s, revealing a new line of DualSense controllers and PlayStation 5 console covers with transparent materials. Dubbed the Prism Collection, it will come in three distinct glossy colors: Flare Orange, Emerald Green, and Graphite Gray.  Preorders will open on November 10 through the PlayStation Direct store ahead of a February 4, 2027 rollout.

Sony says the design was inspired by the PS5 design team's interest in giving the console and its accessories a transparent look while also showing off the hardware beneath the protective surface. Flare Orange has a "bold and vibrant aesthetic," Emerald Green offers an "elegant" finish, and Sony says a PS5 will look "refined" with a Graphite Gray cover.

"We know how much our fans have been looking forward to the return of transparent controllers," Leo Cardoso and Satoshi Aoyagi from Sony's Color, Material, and Finish design team said in a press statement. "We wanted to bring back the iconic see-through trend of the late '90s in a fresh, modern way that complements the PS5's industrial design. "The high-gloss clear finish extends across the back of the controller, offering a look at the technology that powers the DualSense controller while maintaining a sleek, monochromatic look. The metallic finish on the middle cover brings the contrasting surfaces together for a premium appearance that feels consistent with the PS5 generation."

The Prism Collection DualSense controllers have an MSRP of $85 each, while the PS5 console covers are priced at $75 each. If you missed it, Sony also launched limited-edition Marathon and Gran Turismo DualSense controllers this year, and Marvel's Wolverine fans can grab a new PS5 console cover and matching DualSense controller in striking yellow or adamantium-inspired silver, complete with claw marks.
